items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 19 November, the Government intends to move an urgency motion to progress
a number of bills that are on the Order Pa per, including the Social Housing Reform
(Housing Restructuring and Tenancy Matt ers Amendment) Bill and the Financial
Reporting Bill.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I wonder whether the Leader of the
House could indicate whether the Government  expects there to be question time during
urgency.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The Government has had
question time through all of its bouts of urge ncy since coming to office. I imagine that
discussions over the next couple of days with other parties in the Hous e will lead to a
similar result.
Better Public Services Targets—Purpose and Impact
1. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Finance: How is
the Government’s Better P ublic Services programme contributing to a stronger
economy?
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN (Asso ciate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of
the Minister of Finance : Delivering Better Public Services has been a focus of the
Government for the past 5 years. With th e Government representing around one-quarter
of the real economy, it is important that Government agencies focus on achieving
results for users of public services while at the same time delivering value for money for
taxpayers. The Prime Minister last year identified 10 challenging Better Public Services
results to address some of New Zealand’s mo st important issues over the next 4 to 5
years, such as reducing crime, reducing long-term welfare depe ndency, and reducing
educational underachievement.
Simon O’Connor : Why has the Government made the Better Public Services
programme one of its four priorities?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The Government take s the view that New
Zealanders are entitled to the most effective and efficient public services that can be
delivered. The result areas are focused on improving Kiwis’ quality of life and getting
better results for taxpayers. We have seen, for example, that the number of people
continuously receiving a working-age benefit for over 12 months has fallen by almost
3,500 since March last year to 74,600. The target is 55,000 by 2017.
Simon O’Connor : Has the Government’s focus on improving public services had
any impact on public satisfaction and trust in those services?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Yes, indeed. The quarterly Kiwis Count survey
into New Zealanders’ satisfaction with their public services has shown a significant
increase from an overall score of 68 percent when National came to office to 73 percent
now. At the same time, the survey shows a remarkable 10 percent increase in Kiwis’
trust in public servants, from an overall score of 67 percent when National took office to
77 percent today.

State-owned Assets, Sales—Air New Zealand
2. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister of Finance:
Can he rule out the partial sale of Air New Zealand proceeding prior to 30 November
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN (Asso ciate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of
the Minister of Finance : No final decisions around the timing of the reduction in the
Government’s 73 percent holding in Air New Zealand have been made.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why is he so worried of the outcome of the referendum that he
is sneakily selling off Air New Zealand as quickly as he can?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: We are not worried about the result of the
referendum, although we do know th at it is a waste of $9 mill ion of public money, and,
actually, we made our commitments in this whole area very public at the 2011 general
election. As was said by Russel Norman, th at election was a referendum on the whole
mixed-ownership model, and National won the election.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why, then, is the Government  planning to sell off Air New
Zealand in blocks to institutions and brokers rather than the so-called Kiwi mums and
dads whom he promised at the election would be at the front of the queue?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The first thing is th at no decision has been
made. The second issue is that those shares  are already trading on the market. It is
fundamentally different from those two initia l public offerings that  have progressed so
far, so the sale structure is going to be very different.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What does Air New Zealand tell us about the benefits of the
Government’s mixed-ownership programme?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Air New Zealand is lis ted on the New Zealand
and Australian stock exchanges. For the last  12 years the Governme nt has held a stake
in Air New Zealand of around three-quarter s of the company. That makes Air New
Zealand a very good working example of a mixed-ownership company. It also
demonstrates the benefits and disciplines of  a sharemarket listing. I would like to thank
the former Minister of Finance Michae l Cullen for leading the way on the mixed-
ownership model. It is one of the very few good decisions made by the last Labour
Government.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Can the Minister assure the House that Air New Zealand will be
at least 85 percent New Zealand - owned after the sell-down process is completed?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The first thing to say is that no final decisions
about Air New Zealand have been made. The s econd thing is that we have always said
that in the mixed-ownership model, in the fl oat of these assets—in this case, the sell
down—we are going for 85 percent Kiwi-owned.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why did the National Government  say when it made citizens
initiated referenda the law in 1993 that this  was “to give our pe ople a greater voice …”
and bring in “a more meaningful way to asce rtain the views of [the ] people.”, that the
citizens initiated referenda la w is “a sign of the vigour of  our democracy.” , and that it
does not want to “suppress that voice with  subject-matter limitatio ns,”; and, further,
why is it that those lofty ambitions were tossed out the window around the time of the
asset sales programme?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The first thing is that I was not around in 1993.
The second thing is that when that member said “ambitions were tossed out the
window”, the person who tossed them out was Helen Clark. The trouble with those
members opposite is that they pick and c hoose on binding referenda. So when the
smacking referendum came back and said that 87 percent of New Zealanders wanted it
reversed, those members ignored it. But now that they think they might get some sort of
14 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14703
result on the next one, they are suddenly very keen on the idea of referenda. The other
point that I would make is th at the referendum has not yet been held, but it is a waste of
$9 million worth of taxpayers’ money. You and they are both responsible for that gross
waste of money, and it will not change a thing.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Can the Minister tell us who the Prime Minister was in 2009
when the so-called smacking referendum ha ppened, and who was the Prime Minister,
the leader of the Government, who made a decision to take no action as a result of that
referendum?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am struggling to see how that has much ministerial responsibility
connected to the question, but I will allow—[Interruption] Order! I will allow the—

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The issue of relevance is
that the Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not—

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: —raised it in his answer to the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not need—w ell, I appreciate the attempt of assistance
from the member, but I do not need it. On this  occasion I have said that the question is
in order, and I will leave it to the Minister to respond.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: We all know the answer to that question. But
the other thing we do know is  that the economic suicide bombers of the Green Party
would, if they got the chance, be bursting into the Cabinet room—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the Minister please resume his seat? I have another
point of order from Dr Russel Norman.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The Minister did not
attempt to answer the question. Then, he star ted a diatribe about the Green Party. It has
nothing to do with the Green Party.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The difficulty I have with this point of order is that the
Minister was attempting to answer the que stion when the member Dr Russel Norman
rose to his feet and interrupted the answer. Until the answer is completed, I cannot rule
on whether the question has been adequately addressed or not.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: We all know the answer to that question, but
we also know that if the Green Party got hol d of the Treasury benches, the Green Party
members would be going out and printing billi ons of dollars to try to buy these assets
back. I challenge them to deny it.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can you please explain to
me how this has anything to do with the question I asked?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: With some difficulty, but I actua lly have difficulty understanding
the exact question the member asked anyway. If the member—[ Interruption] Order!
The member asked what was, without doubt , a political question. He is unhappy with
the answer. That is not my business. If the member wants to tease it out further, then the
opportunity exists for the member to use further supplementaries.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was
completely in order. It was allowed by you, it referenced the comment that the Minister
made as to who ignored an earlier citizens initiated referendum, and it asked him to
confirm which Prime Minister it was. It was a very simple question. It was in order and
it has not been addressed.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have already ruled that the question has been addressed, maybe
not to the satisfaction of the member, but the question—[ Interruption] Order! If the
member wants to stay for the balance of quest ion time, I would be grateful if he would
not interject while I am on my feet. The que stion has been addressed. I accept that it
may not be to the satisfaction of either th e member who asked the question or the Hon
14704 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Nov 2013
David Parker. That is then a matter for teasing out with further supplementary
questions.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just clarify, before I accept th is point of order, that it is an
absolutely fresh point of order?

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: No, you cannot clarify that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, then, the member would—[ Interruption] Order! The member
will resume his seat. If the member is going to continue to question decisions I make, he
leaves me no option but to ask the member to  leave the Chamber. If it is a fresh point—
[Interruption] Order! If it is a fresh point of orde r, I am happy to accept it, but I have
ruled on that particular matter and that is final.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek a ruling from you in
general terms that is related to this quest ion. If a member asks a Minister a factual
question that has an answer that is factual,  and the Minister knows the answer to that
question and can state it with a simple fact, is it a requirement that the Minister answer
with that fact?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, indeed it is. If a question is asked that is absolutely fair,
concise, and simple, and it is one that I would expect the Minister to be able to answer, I
would then expect the Minister to answer it.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. Just an additional clarification
on the ruling—is it acceptable for a Minister  to give the answer “We all know the
answer …” in response to a very specific factual question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: To a very specific question, maybe not, but to the question that was
asked, yes, I have ruled that that is the case.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of or der, Mr Speaker. I want to raise with you a
slightly different issue, but it is related to the answer that the Minister gave, and it
extends to the issue of ministerial responsibil ity. It is well established in the Standing
Orders and in the Speakers’ rulings that Mi nisters do not have responsibility for the
policies of other parties or for what other parties might do if they became Government.
What is increasingly becoming a practice at the moment is that Ministers are standing
up and giving a very brief answer to a question and then saying “But if that party was in
Government,” and then saying a whole lot of other things. Previously, Speakers have sat
Ministers down when they got to that point, without letting them go on, because they do
not have any responsibility for that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think that point is a reasonable one. There are occasions when I do
sit Ministers down when they attempt to attack  another party. But, at the end of the day,
this is a political debating chamber, and th ere will be times when political barbs are
traded from one side to the other.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Does your ruling mean
that if the way to get a question answered is to ask a further supplementary question,
questioners on this side of the House will ge t an extra supplementary question, or does
it just use up their time?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On occasions—as the member will have observed, on many
occasions—I may well give an extra supplem entary question. But th e point that I am
making to the member and to all members of  the House is that if a supplementary
question is asked, on many, many occasions th e member who asked that question may
not be happy with the answer . That has been happening sin ce I arrived in this House.
The way to then make progress is not to sta nd to one’s feet and expect the Speaker to
rule on the adequacy of the answer, provide d the question has been addressed. The way
to do it is to ask searching, perceptive supplementary questions and to attempt to get the
correct answer.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Who was the Prime Minister when the citizens initiated
referendum was held in respect of th e anti-smacking issue, and who was the
Government that ignored the majority recomm endation of that referendum, all of which
were referred to by the Minister in his answer to an earlier supplementary question?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The initial question is
about the partial sale of Air New Zealand proceeding prior to 30 November 2013.
Although the Minister might have commen ted on a coming referendum, to now be
allowing a question to the Minister about what  is simply historical fact seems to me
quite unreasonable and a waste of members’ time.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not need any assistance on this  particular point. The Hon Gerry
Brownlee is right. It does not  bear a lot of resemblance to the initial question, but the
members in their further supplementary questions, and in the answers given by the
Minister, have talked about ot her citizens initiated referenda. On this occasion I invite
the Hon David Parker to re-ask his question, and it will be answered.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Who was the Prime Minister at the
time of the citizens initiated referendum in respect of the smacking issue, and who was
the Prime Minister and who was in Government when that referendum was ignored?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I do not have that information with me, but if
you would like to submit the question in writing, the Minister will get back to you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A point of order is being raised, and it will be heard in
silence.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can a Minister who prev iously said that everybody
knows the answer but who apparently does not know it himself not be treating this
House with anything other than contempt? This  is an awful waste of Parliament’s time,
and it makes us look foolish in front of the public, which comes naturally to some
members, but some of us do not like it.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I am sure that you will find that the Minister has moved from
that clear statement initially that everyone knows the answer to that . After such a long
period of time with the House being so intere sted in this matter, he has begun to doubt
himself.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Again, for the benefit of the Rt Hon Winston Peters, it is not
for me to judge the adequacy of the answer. It is for the members of this House and the
public to judge the adequacy of the answer  that was given. But the answer given was
satisfactory.
Schools, Canterbury—Building and Redevelopment Projects
3. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Education
items.text: What recent announcements has she made on repairi ng, rebuilding and
renewing schools in Christchurch?
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery) on
behalf of the Minister of Education : Today, with the support of the Minister for
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, the Minister of Educatio n announced that 80 percent
of classrooms across greater Christchurch will be modernised within 10 years, changing
the way children and young peopl e learn. The final business case, which was released
today, outlines the schedule fo r the rebuilding, repairing, and renewing of 115 State
schools across greater Christchur ch. The Government is inves ting over $1 billion in a
10-year programme of restoring and renewing schools in the greater Christchurch area.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What impact will this have on schools in Christchurch?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Schools in Christchurch have already been severely
impacted by the earthquakes. This business case today, though, indicates that 13 schools
14706 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Nov 2013
will be built on new sites, 10 schools will be rebuilt on existing sites, 34 schools will be
fully redeveloped, and 58 schools will have modernising redevelopments. In other
words, it means the construction of over 1,200 new classrooms and the repair of more
than 1,200 others, creating improved learning spaces that are fit for modern teaching
practices.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: How much of the $1 billion announced today will come from money
the schools were already due to receive in the form of regular property funding, leaky
buildings remediation, and insurance payouts?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There will be various amounts in the $1.1 billion that
have those component issues attached to th em. I am not in a position today to give him
those exact figures, but, certain ly, if he wishes to put a question down in writing, then
those breakdowns could be provided.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Will schools being built or rebuilt in Christchurch be built using
public-private partnerships; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There is certainly a desire  to have some of those
schools built using that model. That would, of course, free up  principals from having to
be property managers to being the educators that they are so well trained to be.
Climate Change—Minister’s Statements
4. MOANA MACKEY (Labour)  to the Minister of Transport : Does he stand by
all his statements?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, as long as they are
properly reported and in the right context.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that “I think climate change is
something that has happened always, so to simply come up and say it is man-made is an
interesting prospect.”; if so, is he saying th at the nearly 50 percent increase in global
greenhouse gas emissions from transport in th e last 25 years has played no role in
causing our planet to heat up at an unprecedented rate?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, no, and I am unsure.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: When he described man-made climate change as being “an
interesting prospect” was he aware that  anthropogenic climate change, to which
emissions from transport are a major contributor, is actually not a new concept, and that
thousands of scientists worldwide have been  working on this small issue for decades; if
not, does that allay his concerns that someone simply came up with the idea?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, and no.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Does he agree with his colleague the Hon Tim Groser that to deny
man-made climate change you would “have to be denying reality”; and if he does not
agree, then how can the public have any c onfidence that his Gove rnment is taking
seriously the need to reduce our emissions from transport?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, and if they look at ou r record in tr ansport, in
regulation, and in the construc tion of roads that reduce emissions, then of course they
will agree with our position.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Does he appreciate how embarra ssing it is in 2013 to have a New
Zealand Minister of Transport publicly que stioning the science of climate change—a
Minister who is responsible for policy settings in the sector with the fastest-growing
level of emissions—and will he promise not to do it again?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, there we have it. I said yes, and I stand by my
statements when they are reported in the pr oper context. What we had yesterday was a
bit of a cook-up between TV3 and the Gree ns, attempting to get a result that would
favour the Green Party. Everyone knows that. It was pretty clear. I tell you what—when
you see a reporter bounding towards you and as king a question like that, you always
14 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14707
give an answer that is going to be a little tempered in terms of the madness that comes
from the Greens.
Housing, Affordable—Government Measures
5. PAUL FOSTER-BELL (National)  to the Minister of Housing: What initiatives
has the Government recently taken to assi st first home buyers and ensure more lower-
cost homes are being built?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: This morning we turned the first
sod on the $30 million - plus 150-home redevelopment at P ōmare. This community,
which has had more than its fair share of gang and crime problems, is a good illustration
of why we need to reform our historic ap proach to State housing. The new development
will provide good-quality low-cost homes for sale, which will open the door to
homeownership for 110 families. The remain ing 40 homes will be split between the
community housing providers, like Accessi ble Properties, the Wellington Housing
Trust, and Housing New Zealand. I am confid ent that this remodelled community will
deliver far better social outcomes for the future.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What reports has the Minister ha d on the Government’s initiatives
that took effect on 1 October in expanding the Welcome Home Loan and the KiwiSaver
first-home deposit subsidy?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There has been a big increase  in the number of first-home
buyers accessing Welcome Home Loan lo ans, particularly in Auckland and
Christchurch, where we increased e ligibility by $85,000 and $100,000, respectively.
The numbers have doubled to 47 per week and are at an all-time high since the scheme
was established more than a decade ago. I am also encouraged that three further major
banks that were previously outside the scheme have now applied to join and this will, in
time, expand the number of first-home  buyers accessing the Welcome Home Loan
scheme. Also, the growth in the uptake of  the KiwiSaver first-home deposit subsidy
arises because we have lifted both the income and house pri ce caps. This initiative is
helping first-home buyers and is complemen ting the Reserve Bank concerns about low-
deposit lending.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Why, if his Government is so c oncerned about the housing crisis, has
it, as the Salvation Army has reported t oday, cut the annual ca pital contribution to
Housing New Zealand in half and pulled nearly half a billion dollars in dividends out of
Housing New Zealand, resulting in a net $142 million withdrawal of funds in the middle
of a housing crisis, when there are 4,000 fa milies on waiting lists and Government
agencies are referring people to live in cam ping grounds; and will he confirm that the
Government has been squeezing the lifeblood out of Housing New Zealand to pay for
National’s tax cuts?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member’s numbers are all wrong. The Government is
investing a record $2.9 billion in Housing Ne w Zealand over the next 3 years, and I
challenge the member opposite to find any period of Labour Government when that sort
of investment took place in Housing New Zealand. The development that we launched
this morning in P ōmare is just a classic example of the major investment that we are
making in improving the quality of our social housing.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I seek leave of the H ouse to table the report  by the Salvation Army,
which details a $142 million—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! Seeking leave to table a document is a
matter of briefly describing the document; it is  not about making a political point. What
I just need to check before I put the leav e is whether it is a document that has been
circulated and is freely available to members of Parliament.
14708 Questions for Oral Answer 14 Nov 2013

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: The report has been released only in the last hour. It is not publicly
available to everybody yet, and it directly pertains to the information that—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The easiest way to move this forward is to accept what the
member has said. I will put the leave. It is over to the House. L eave is sought to table
that particular report. Is there any objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What interest has there been in the Government’s FirstHome
initiative?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There have been 14,000 viewings on the website and over
1,000 phone and email inquiries for the scheme, which is designed to give preference to
first-home buyers of surplus properties in provincial New Zealand. Sales have been
completed in Ōtorohanga, Napier, Marton, Foxton, Levin, Picton, Blenheim, Timaru,
Cromwell, Dunedin, and Invercargill. I have been heartened by letters from first-home
purchasers, like the one I received from a fa mily in Invercargill, which said: “It’s a
dream I never expected to attain, and I will never forget that I’ve been given this
opportunity to own my own home for myself and my son.”
Climate Change—Government Position
6. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
have confidence in all his Ministers?
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery) on
behalf of the Prime Minister: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with the views and have confidence in the
accuracy of the views of his climate change Minister, Tim Groser, who said yesterday
that the evidence of human-induced clim ate change is overwhelming and that you
would have to be denying reality if you did not accept that?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Then does he agree with the views of his Minister of Finance,
who yesterday refused to accept the scientif ic consensus that human-induced climate
change is happening?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: What the Deputy Prime Mini ster was not prepared to
accept were the mad excesses often quoted by the Green Party.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: If the finance Minister refu ses to accept th e science around
climate change, has the Prime Minister asked the finance Minister what he thinks the
explanation for climate change is, and does he believe that it could be the circulation of
the planets that is causing climate change, as Colin Craig seems to think?

views on the science around climate change?

items.text: No. We talk about substantial things, not fairy tales.

items.text: Is the reason his Ministers a nd his Government are promoting
fossil fuel extraction and mining that they do not accept the science of climate change
and hence do not realise that we cannot continue to increase the burning of fossil fuels?

items.text: No. A well-known, noted professor made the point
back in the 1970s that if the world today was to replace with horses all the horsepower

manure.

items.text: It may be difficult for th e member to recognise this,

Institution of Professional Engineers New Zealand—Disciplinary Powers
7. Hon SHANE JONES (Labour) to the Minister for Building and Construction:
Does he agree with IPENZ Chief Executive,  Andrew Cleland, that the Government
needs to give the Institute greater powers to hold their own to account?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.role: Ministe r for Building and Construction

items.text: What has become clear following the collapse  of the CTV Building in 2011 is that the
accountability regime for engineers is woefully  inadequate. I find it  abhorrent that an
engineer found to have done poor  work can still be practising,  even after being stripped
of their Institution of Professional E ngineers New Zealand registration. The
Government is working to drastically improve the occupational regulations of
engineers, and I expect to be able to a nnounce some changes next year. That extensive
work that is under way will determine wh at additional powers the Institution of
Professional Engineers would receive. It mi ght be that the current structure of the
institution, playing all the roles it does, may change as well.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Why has it taken so long for the Institution of Professional
Engineers to step up to the plate, show accountability, and bring this engineer into
where he belongs—the dock, next to the form er chief executive officer of Pike River
Coal?

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.text: First of all, I do not have responsibility directly
for the Institution of Professional Engineer s, but I can tell the member that the
institution itself does not have  very many tools in its tool box to do such . That is why
the whole case of the engineers involved in the CTV Building has been put to the police
and the police are still currently investigating as to whether they will take a prosecution.
I actually do not find it an acceptable regi me where 115 people died in a building that
was illegally designed, built, and certified, an d still no one held accountable. That is
why I think that the regime must change.

items.text: Well, I repeat again that I do not find the current
regime acceptable. I do not think that the curr ent regime is acceptable. That is why we
have been consulting with the engineering profession, bringing an issues paper to the
market early in the new year. We would hop e to have legislativ e changes during the
course of next year and I look forward to the support of members from the other side. In
the mean time I am advised by the Instituti on of Professional Engineers that the only
action it can take is deregist ration, and even that does not prevent an engineer under the

question is why it is that he  is so disconnected from the young people he claims to

MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT (REMUNERATION AND SERVICES) BILL
Third Reading
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Attorney-General)  on behalf of the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: I move, That the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Bill be
now read a third time . The Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill
represents a significant improvement in m odernising the law relating to members’
remuneration and entitlement to services. The bill establishes a new framework for
setting entitlements for members of Par liament and the executive. In doing so, it
implements, subject to some modifications , many of the recommendations in the Law
Commission’s report Review of the Civil List Act 1979: Members of Parliament and
Ministers. The bill repeals the Civil List Act 1979—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to
interrupt the member. It is a longstanding convention that members should not conduct
conversations in the House unless it is nece ssary to do so and then only so as to not
disturb the proceedings. Would members l eaving the Chamber please do so and show
some courtesy to the member who is trying to address the House. It is good conduct and
it is being considerate of others.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Thank you. I will not name and shame Mr
Twyford on this occasion. The bill modernises and modifi es the law relating to the
salaries and allowances of MPs; support services provided  for MPs, Ministers, and
certain electoral candidates; annuities and other benefits and privileges for former Prime
Ministers; and benefits and privileges for former members of Parliament.
As members know, the bill makes the Remuneration Authority rather than the
Speaker responsible for determining accommod ation services for MPs and Ministers,
and also travel services for family member s of MPs. It makes the Speaker responsible
for setting directions on travel and communication serv ices for MPs and party and
member support funding. Thirdly, it makes th e Minister responsib le for Ministerial
Services responsible for determining any addi tional travel services  for Ministers over
and above those set by the Speaker for MPs. This division of responsibility reflects what
are intersecting interests here, one interest being that of having en titlements determined
independently from those who receive them, an d the other being the democratic interest
in the proper operation of the House and the ability of its members to carry out their
functions.
The bill also updates the legislative fram ework for the setting of salaries and
allowances for MPs and Minister s. It addresses the current gap in the law relating to
authorisation of the starting date for paymen t of salaries to MPs who enter Parliament
mid-term, following the vacancy of a seat held by a list member of Parliament. The
proposed amendment will allow these members to  be paid lawfully. The bill validates
the commencement of salaries paid to mid-term list MPs since 1996, and it is a measure
that will not incur further costs to the Crown.
14718 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
The bill also substantially increases the financial penalty for MPs who are absent
from the House without permission, with de ductions starting after 3 days’ absence and
the amount deducted reflecting the member’s actu al salary rather than the salary of an
ordinary MP. The financial penalty for absent  members used to be based on an ordinary
MP’s salary. Now, in the bill, it is based on the actual salary of the member and, as I
said, it commences after 3 days of absence, rather than 9 days’ absence in the original
proposal.
The bill introduces a financial penalty for members who are suspended from the
House. The clauses covering financial penalties for members suspended from the House
are new and reflect a recommendation made by the Standing Orders Committee.
The bill also provides for entitlements to services to be determined in a way that
takes into account the partic ular requirements of member s with physical or sensory
impairments. As all MPs are aware, in recen t years there have been a number of moves
to improve transparency around the costs of the House, and this bill codifies those
moves. It imposes a statutory obligation on the general manager of Parliamentary
Service and the Department of Internal Affairs to publish quarterly reports on travel and
accommodation costs for both MPs and Ministers. It also imposes a statutory obligation
on the Clerk of the House to publish quarterly  reports on MPs’ and parties’ use of the
interparliamentary relations programme.
The bill also addresses the operation of  the scheme providing certain former
members with entitlements. As re commended by the Law Commission, the bill
legislates for the former member travel en titlements of MPs elected before—take note,
Mr Assistant Speaker—1999, thereby making those entitlements transparent and able to
be changed only by legislative amendment. It introduces a statutory regime that sets out
how these travel entitlements can be lost, including for various offences. It also imposes
a statutory obligation on Parliamentary Serv ice to publish on an annual basis the travel
expenses of former MPs.
In conclusion, this bill makes a number of very sensible  changes, and these are done
to ensure that the House and its members are properly supported in a way that maintains
confidence in the integrity of Parliament. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Can I commend the Minister Chris
Finlayson for his words in the third r eading of the Members of Parliament
(Remuneration and Services) Bill, and also acknowledge the members of the
Government Administration Committee, who ha ve worked pretty hard on this bill. I
think we asked for two extensions in order to get the agreement of all members of the
select committee. There are three part ies in the Government Administration
Committee—National, Labour, and the Greens—a nd all parties agreed completely in
the end. Actually, during the process we ha d quite a lot of differing opinions, even
within each party, because some of these i ssues are not as black and white or as
straightforward as some matters are. We also  had pretty impressive contributions to our
deliberation, including from the former Speaker of the House, the Rt Hon Sir Lockwood
Smith, now resident in London, who made a ve ry considered and robust contribution to
the thinking of the committee. I want to ac knowledge his contribu tion, as well as the
contribution of the Clerk of the House and others who also made very considered
contributions.
The primary driver of this legislation is to modernise the regime under which
members of Parliament’s remuneration a nd services are provided, and not only to
address what are some clear anomalies or gaps in the system but also to improve
transparency. I think without doubt that that was an issue on whic h all members of the
Government Administration Committee, whic h I am privileged to chair, reached
agreement immediately. We understand from our own constituents that when public
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14719
money is used, when taxpayers’ money is funding the operation of Parliament, there has
to be the highest level of transparency in th e use of that money. I am very pleased that
this legislation has progressed that transparency even further than the original proposals.
It certainly has been the case in the last 10 or  15 years particularly, I suppose, that there
has been more transparency in the use of public money. I do not know whether the
public is yet at a time when they can say: “Yes, this feels right, and we understand what
the money is used for.”, but I certainly hope that after the passing of this legislation, that
transparency will increase the public confiden ce in the operation of Parliament, because
that is pretty important.
The next round of decisions that we considered were who made determinations about
remuneration and support services that memb ers of Parliament and their parliamentary
staff and out-of-Parliament staff may receive—whether that determination should be
made by the Speaker of the House, or whether that determination should be made by the
Remuneration Authority. We changed, by unanimous agreement of the select
committee, the provision in regard to the tr avel for members of Parliament. We agreed
that that would remain the responsibility of the Speaker, and this is for a very simple
reason. It is because we view the travel that members of Parliament undertake as being a
fundamental part of the work of a member of Parliament. For those of us who live
outside Wellington—thankfully—and, indeed, outside this island, we know that it is our
responsibility to come to Parliament every we ek. That is part of the travel that we
undertake as part of our job.
It was our view that the work-related require ment of a member of Parliament to be
able to travel to perform their duties—not ju st travelling from home  to Parliament but
also travelling from home or Parliament to  other duties, either as a Minister, as a
spokesperson, as a National Party backbencher, or as an Opposition spokesperson—is
really critical to not only fulfilling your job as a member of Parliament but also ensuring
that we have a healthy democracy. We ca nnot have a democracy that flourishes in
Wellington and ignores the rest of the country. So it was our view that the proper place
in which that determination should be made was with the Speaker. We did not,
however, feel the same in regard to the trav el that family members are able to access.
We agree that it is a very important supporting part of being a member of Parliament to
have family members able to travel to pr ovide support on various occasions, but we did
not agree that it was fundamental to your  job. Therefore, we agreed that the
determination of travel for family memb ers should properly go to the Remuneration
Authority.
With the provision of support se rvices, we believe that that  is, again, a core role of
fulfilling your duties as a member of Parliament, and it should, therefore, be a
determination of the Speaker. I am really de lighted that this bill clarifies that the
funding of support services for any member of Parliament is the responsibility of
Parliament and not the responsibility of th e individual party to which the member who
needs those support services belongs. We  have had instances—over the last, well
perhaps since Invercargill was held by a Labour  member of Parliame nt, so it goes back
quite a long way—where members of Parliament have a physical or sensory impairment
and may require different support services in  order that they can  perform their full
function as a member of Parliament compar ed with other members. There has been a
debate in recent times about whether thos e support services for a member with a
physical or sensory impairment should be f unded by the party that that member belongs
to, or whether it is the responsibility of Pa rliament. We have kicked that out the door
and said that without doubt this is the responsibility of Parliament. I hope that this gives
a really clear message to all disabled New Zealanders that they would be welcome in
this Parliament as contributing members, rega rdless of what party they were elected to
14720 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
represent, and that Parliament would consid er it our responsibility to provide proper
support services so that they are able to perform their duties.
There are a couple of other poin ts that I just want to dr aw to the attention of the
House. I mentioned right at the beginning our  very quick and unanimous agreement on
the point of recognising how th e public feels about their ta xpayers’ money being used
for these purposes—to fund the operation of Parliament, including not only the salaries
of members of Parliament and their support services but also the allowances that former
members of Parliament get. That is often an  issue of contention. It was our view that
this was a very important area in terms of improving transparency of the use of those
funds. So the travel of former members of  Parliament will now become part of the
public record. Again, I do hope that members of the public see that as a good thing. It is
their money, not our money, and how it is used  should be a matter of public record, so
that people can then make th eir contribution known in a deba te about whether that is a
fair use or a good use.
I am sure that many people in our constituencies quite often wonder what we do
when we come to Parliament, as, indeed, wi ll the thousands and thousands of people
who will be watching this debate on television. They will look around the room and
they will see many seats that do not have a member sitting on them. They will wonder
whether the person has knocked off early and gone home, or whether they have gone
down Lambton Quay to do some shopping. What are they doing if they are not sitting in
the House? Well, we know, as members of Parliament, that the commitments outside
the Chamber are real. We have other meetings that we all attend and they are meetings
that are important to us, for various reasons. But for a member of Parliament just to go
AWOL and not turn up at all is not acceptabl e to any of us, so we have increased the
penalties that those AWOL me mbers will have to pay. We have linked it directly to
their salary, so if a Minister goes AWOL, they will not be penalised on the basis of their
salary being a backbencher’s salary; they will be penalised as a percentage of the
ministerial salary they rece ive. That should give a very  clear message that when
members of Parliament are elected to be representatives, they should turn up and do
their job.
The same applies for members of Parliament who are suspended for bad behaviour.
Fortunately, we do not get that very often. I did think during question time today that
there might be a bit of a clear-out, but, in  the end, there was no t; the Speaker dropped
his focus on removing some members. But if  a member is suspended from the House,
then we think there should be a financial pena lty attached to that, and that is included in
the provisions here. Clause 14A in the bill came directly from a recommendation of the
Standing Orders Committee.
I think that the work that we have done ha s been pretty rigorous. It was not always
black and white. There were some differenc es in consideration, but I think we got
quality submissions. I think that we all worked really hard to make sure that the public
funds that are used to s upport our democracy in New Zealand have not only a fair
process but also a transparent process. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to stand for the third reading of
this particular bill, the Members of Parlia ment (Remuneration and Services) Bill. I felt
that the Attorney-General, Mr Finlayson, gave a wonderful introduction to the third
reading—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: He thought so too.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: —yes; indeed, it is a very serious bill—and it was
followed equally well by the speech made by the chair of the Government
Administration Committee, Ruth Dyson. It has b een a pleasure to work with her as her
deputy on this particular issue.
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14721
I guess one could see this bill as a con tinuum—a continuum of change, of updating,
of looking ahead, and of bringing the services  that we have in Parliament, which are
entirely for the nation, to a level that is  commensurate with modern travel, modern
working ethics, and modern communications sy stems. Things change. In the past there
have been all sorts of different ways of  establishing processes, procedures, and
entitlements for MPs.
There used to be a time, of course—and I am  sure the Speaker can correct me if I am
wrong; not that I am suggesting it is with in his purview or memory—when MPs simply
stayed here for a whole block of time duri ng a year, completed the business, and then
went back and worked in their electorates,  rather than the weekly business that we
transact now. Who knows? With electronic communication, we may well be able to
change further in the future.
This bill has been a refreshing bill to be pa rt of, and I am very pleased that we have
addressed this during my time in Parliament a nd that I have been able to participate in
the process. This Government is committed to  having MPs’ and Ministers’ entitlements
determined in a transparent, independent, a nd non-partisan manner. It is important that
the public has confidence in the regime fo r setting entitlements. The bill puts more
power in the hands of independent deci sion-makers appointed to do the job. The
Speaker and the Government have already ta ken several steps to improve transparency
around entitlements, and this bill takes that a step further and sets it in legislation.
One of the features that I think was particularly important was the select committee
process. Members of the Government Admini stration Committee were particularly well
advised during the process of this bill. The submissions came from a range of people
with much experience in the matter of how Pa rliament runs, and th e officials available
to the committee were drawn from several di sciplines. I think I speak for all committee
members when I say that the advice we rece ived was uniformly of a very high calibre
indeed.
Changes were introduced to the bill as it progressed through the select committee.
This is actually what select committees are there to do. There has been some criticism in
some media that—gosh—the select committee ha s made changes. Well, it would be of
concern if the select committee did not make ch anges as a result of its consideration of
the submissions it received. That is why we do not need two Houses of Parliament; we
just have the one, because select committees fulfil such an important part of the process.
I might make the point that I think it is  particularly important to have full
involvement of all parties in the process that select committees go through. I am always
a little concerned when everything seems to be completed in the select committee
process, which is the real place to ha ve debate, and parties then put forward
Supplementary Order Papers. The select committee is the place to have the debate—
when the committee is working together with the advisers, and, after the advisers have
gone, when the committee makes its own considerations. For parties to then come
forward with Supplementary Order Papers that we have not ha d the opportunity to
debate is a disappointment, and it did occur w ith this bill. However, the bill reaches its
completion in the third reading, and I am ve ry, very happy to give it my support. Thank
you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Christopher Hipkins.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That is what my mother called me,
normally when I had been very poorly behaved.
I do have to disagree with something that Chris Auchinvole said when he said that he
was delighted to speak on the third reading of this bill, the Members of Parliament
(Remuneration and Services) Bill . I do not feel quite the same  level of joy. It would be
14722 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
fair to say that there is not a huge number of MPs queuing up to speak on this particular
topic, because there is a fa ir degree of public cynicism, I think, when it comes to MPs
talking about their own pay and rations, if you like. I thi nk, potentially, that if you look
at the situation historically, often with some good reason the public would look on us
debating these matters and talk ing about how hard we work, and how we need this and
how we need that, with a degree of cynicism.
I think that if you look back over the histor y of this debate, sometimes it has actually
been fair and justified. I think that is absolu tely right. I think that, over time, MPs have,
if you like, responded to the publ ic pressure and pub lic criticism of those matters, and
have put in place steps to ensure that ther e is a degree of independence in how many of
these issues are decided. We do not vote on ou r own salaries, contrary, I think, to what
many in the public would think. We do not de termine our own salaries. We actually get
very little say in how much we get paid. I do want to say, however,  that I love being a
member of Parliament. I feel incredibly privileged to have the honour of being a
member of Parliament. I certainly do not think I am poorly recompensed for being a
member of Parliament. All I ask for is that we are given the tools we need to do the job
we are put here to do by the voters of New Zealand, and that  we are able to do that job
effectively.
I do not expect to get rich by being a member  of Parliament, but nor do I want to see
a situation evolve where you have to be rich in order to become a member of
Parliament. I think it is very, very important that in this House of Representatives we do
have a genuinely representative Parliament. I th ink that if we sort of erode a lot of the
support that is available to members of Parlia ment to the extent that many in the public
would like to see happen, we will create  a situation where somebody needs to be
independently wealthy and able to support themselves before  they can actually function
effectively as a member of Parliament and a representative of the people. I would hate
to see Parliament become that way. I do not expect to become hugely wealthy by being
an MP, but nor do I think I should have to go out and become wealthy before I can
come here and represent the people who elect me.
I think there have been some really important aspects to this debate that I do not want
to overlook. Metiria Turei is here and I am sure she is going to be speaking after me.
One of the points that Metiria Turei raised in  the debate in the Committee stage earlier
in the week was the need to distinguish betw een what is of personal benefit to members
of Parliament and what is a work-related expe nse. In principle, I want to say that I
absolutely do agree with that. The reality, t hough, is that it is qui te difficult, in many
instances, to determine that, particularly when it comes to travel. On the issue of
accommodation and on the issue of salary, where there is personal benefit, that has been
removed from parliamentarians’ hands and given to the Remuneration Authority, which
is independent, and I think that is the right thing to do.
The issue of travel is very difficult because members of Parliament travel not just to
and from Parliament but to and from their hom es to other parts of the country for work-
related reasons, and it is sometimes difficult to distinguish what is work-related travel
and what is personal travel. For example—I will give a nice easy one—a member of
Parliament from Auckland flies to Wellington each week to be here as a parliamentarian
and to be in the House. From time to time members of Parliament will need to go home
during the week for family-related reasons. Is that personal travel or is that work-related
travel? They are here for work but they ha ve to return home for personal reasons. How
would we classify that? If someone is at the other end of the country—say, in
Dunedin—on work-related business, and then they might have a gap of a day where
they go back home and then they return to Dunedin 2 days later to do some other work-
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14723
related thing, is that work-related travel or is that personal travel? They are returning to
their home for personal reasons.
It is sometimes very difficult to distinguish between what is work related and what is
personal, when it comes to travel. In many, many other thi ngs it is very easy to
distinguish. When it comes to our salaries, it is  a personal benefit. That is what we get
paid back for the jobs we do.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: I hope it’s work related.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Well, we are earning it, but th ere is an element of personal
benefit in earning money. I do not think anyone would disagree with that. So I think that
it is fair that that be determined independent ly of us, but I think that in the case of
travel, that can be quite difficult.
The other thing about travel is that I agree with transparency in so far as MPs’ travel
costs are concerned, but I think we need to be  careful about the extent to which we take
that. I think that the tran sparency we have around trav el now has already changed
behaviour probably to what it was before I ev er became an MP. I have been an MP for
only 5 years. I think that prio r to that, MPs could have free,  unfettered travel anywhere
around the country. There was no transparency  and accountability around that. Now the
total amount that MPs spend on travel each year is disclosed. I think that is probably the
appropriate level for disclosure.
If we got into the situation where every indivi dual flight or every individual taxi fare
had to be disclosed, we would quickly find ourselves in the position where members of
Parliament would become less accessible to the public because every individual visit a
member of Parliament did would have to be justified publicly, one at a time. People
would stop doing things because they would not  want to disclose the individual details
of all the things they were doing. I think that would be unfortunate. So I think the
disclosure level we have got now, where we are disclosing how much is spent on travel,
is the appropriate level, and it does encourage members of Parliament to be as efficient
as possible in making their travel arrangement s. I think we have got  that balance about
right.
The other thing I also want to  make clear is the safeguards that have been built in to
this legislation for the taxpayer. If any one of the things that takes place under this bill
does amount to a personal benefit to memb ers of Parliament, then the Remuneration
Authority must take that into consideration in determining the salaries of members of
Parliament. Basically, what it says is that if  parliamentarians appropriate for themselves
something that has a personal benefit, then the Remuneration Authority will take that
personal benefit into account and offset that against the salary, and the salary will be
deducted accordingly. So it is a safeguard to stop—I am sure it would not happen in this
Parliament—any future Parliaments from basi cally awarding themselves some personal
benefit in addition to their sa lary, because it will be offset against their salary. I think
that is a good safeguard for th e taxpayer to know that there are protections in place to
stop that sort of thing from happening.
There are a few things in this bill that I think are welcome and overdue and normally,
I guess, in any other place would just be d ealt with by an employer. But, here, because
of the unusual employment relationships we have, we do have to have legislation. The
“AWOL” clause, as I refer to it, has b een mentioned several times—members of
Parliament being absent without leave for a period of time. There have been very few
provisions that have been able to discourage that behaviour and penalise that behaviour,
and this bill deals with that. I mentioned my  solution to that in the Committee stage of
this debate, which is that I believe, speak ing as a former whip, that some form of
microchipping or ankle bracelets would be an appropriate monitoring mechanism to
ensure that members of Parliament were doing—electrified ankl e bracelets would be
14724 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
even better to incentivise the appropriate behaviour by members of Parliament. But I
have yet to have widespread support for that idea from my colleagues, unfortunately.
I also believe that in the cases where memb ers of Parliament are suspended from the
House, their salaries should be docked. I wa nt to be clear, though, that that does not
mean that they get turfed out of the Chamber for naughty behaviour and they go back to
their offices and continue working. Suspen sion from Parliament means they are named,
and being named means there has to be a vot e in the House. It happens rarely, but I
think it is important that when it happens there is some consequence for that, because
that encourages MPs to lift their behaviour and to avoid getting named by the Speaker.
Now there is provision in this legislation to ensure that their salaries will be deducted
accordingly if they find themselves in that position.
The final clause that I want to mention, wh ich I think is long ove rdue, is the ability
now in this legislation to  cancel under certain circumst ances the travel and other
entitlements for former members of Parliament . There is a lot of public disquiet about
the fact that former members of Parliament  actually get travel entitlements once they
cease being members of Parliament. Again, I want to make it clear that that has
changed. The world has changed. It relate s only to an ever-d iminishing group of
members of Parliament. Anyone who came in after 1996, I think it was, does not qualify
for that any more. We do not have the gold-plated superannuation scheme that they used
to have. A lot of those things have gone now . There is a lot more transparency about it
and I think that that is a welcome thing.
This bill is a step in the right direction. I think we will continue to evolve, continue to
increase the level of transp arency and accountability that members of Parliament have
around these matters, and I think that that is a very positive thing.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. T ēnā
koutou e te Whare. I want to thank Chris Hipki ns and say that I agr ee with a great deal
of what he has just said in the House on the Members of  Parliament (Remuneration and
Services) Bill. I think he is absolutely right that the process by which we are increasing
the transparency and the independence in the setting of MPs’ allowances and expenses
and salaries is a very good th ing. It is continually evolvi ng, and we have had a great
deal more change over the last 5 years than  we probably had in the previous 30 years.
So, clearly, Parliament is doing its best to respond to public issues, re spond to media
scrutiny, and respond to a modern environment. We are in the 21 st century now. We
operate in a different environment than we did last century.
I agree absolutely about the concern of  representation. This is a House of
Representatives. Wealth is not a criterion for entry here and should never be. It has been
in the past, I think, but it should never be ever again. Anyone from any walk of life
should be able to come to this House based on their community support, and on the
nation’s support, to represent their people and their interests here.
I would disagree with Chris just on one issue, really, which is around the public view
of MPs and MPs’ expenses. I have more optimism, actually, about the public view. Iain
Lees-Galloway raises his eyebrows, and understandably so. But I would just note for the
House that we have been debating this legislation around MPs expenses and allowances,
which is of intense interest to a few, and there has been very lit tle public discourse or
discussion about the debate that we are havi ng and are about to c onclude. We are doing
so in a week where the New Zealand Herald has run three stories on MPs’ expenses,
and other media have been doing rolling stories, as well. There has been a little bit of
heat around that, but nothing like what  we saw in 2009 and 2010. We also have the
issue that people tell me about—that the Remuneration Authority is soon to announce
what MPs’ pay will be for the next 12 mont hs—and yet there has not been this great
public fury. There has been a public disc ussion. There have be en different views
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14725
expressed, and expressed publicly—expressed on Twitter, on social media, and in the
news, and people are asked for their views. There is, I agree, some cynicism from the
public about how all of our expenses and a llowances and salaries are set, and our
involvement in all of that. But, again, it is nothing like the public  backlash that we
might have expected in earlier years, and nothing like the public backlash that I think
MPs are concerned about.
I think that the public, in the main, understand that we need to be paid for our job,
and that we need financial resources to do our job and to do our job properly. What they
expect from us in exchange is transparency  on how we use those pub lic resources, that
we do our jobs properly, that we are a good workforce and do what is expected of us,
and that we do not take personal benefit fr om the use of that public money beyond our
pay. It is a perfectly reasonable expectation and there has been a perfectly reasonable, in
my view, debate about this. I am very surprised at how lit tle heat there has been this
week, comparatively speaking. So I have a more optimistic view about the public and
their view about how we are managing this issue, and I do think that it signals very
strongly that there will be further change.
As the House knows, the Green Party did not agree with the travel expenses for MPs
remaining with the Speaker. We preferred th e original bill that came to the House,
which said that the travel expenses would go to the Remuneration Authority, along with
the accommodation allowances and other i ssues. We talked about that at the
Government Administration Committee. We cam e to an agreement that we had got as
far as we could get with that committee. We have put those issues back to this House.
The House decided not to support that view —such is the democratic process. But,
again, there is no great heat in this discussi on. It is simply about  how we are managing
to evolve in taking the steps as far as we can go.
We are very pleased with the changes that the legislation has made—make no
mistake. We are very pleased with the r ecognition of MPs being entitled to support
when they have an impairment that preven ts them from being able to use the same
supports that MPs without impairment get.  We think absolutely that a financial
contribution to managing the barriers that those impairments place on MPs’ engagement
should be the responsibility of the entire or ganisation, and not just of an MP. We are
very pleased that accommodation allowa nces are moving to the Remuneration
Authority. That was raised this week. We are very pleased that the Green Party’s
original proposal for the re lease of our expenses, whic h we started in 2009, has now
been put in legislation. Up until now, it had been a policy. It had not been a legislative
requirement, and now it is. It is  fantastic. That is the proc ess of change. That is what
progress is—the process of change. So that is all great work.
There is still a question—and Chris Hipkins raised this—around how to deal with the
issue of personal benefit from the travel allowance. Chris Hipkins is quite right. If we
were to say that we would keep the trav el allowance in-house under the Speaker, but
that we would restrict it to  being used for parliamentary purposes only, we would have
to have a conversation, a discussion, about what constitutes parliamentary purposes, and
we would need to have that with the publ ic, because there is public interest in
determining how that works. There may be  the construction of rules—or guidelines;
rules, actually, not guidelines —that we would develop to show that we could do our
jobs, do them effectively, represent our commu nities, and return to our homes, which
was the example that was given. All of those things would be within  a set of rules that
we largely agree to by consensus—by all members of the House and by the public. That
is possible. We can have that conversation, and I expect that we will. This is not the end
point. There will be more change and those conversations will get easier over time, just
as this one has been much easier than the last time we talked about these issues.
14726 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
Increasing transparency is great. It is good to  see that in the bill. MPs will always be
under scrutiny.
I would just note one thing of interest to the public—if it is of interest—which is, of
course, that MPs are not employed. We are here by the operation of the law. We are
removed from our role only by the operation of the law. So that is why our salaries, for
example, and the other tools that we need for our jobs are incorporated into the law. We
have no legal structure for our employment , so we are in a very unique situation
compared with any other group of employees an ywhere else in the country, and that is
why so much of this is public. I do not know  about other members, but it seems to me
that often we read about our salary increas es in the newspaper. There are little, small
things like that that make our lives more interesting, and it does bring some real public
transparency into the work that we do.
The Green Party will support this legislation. We see it as a great step. We are very
pleased about the nature of the conversation that has been had ove r this legislation,
particularly given some of the political heat this week, but we do remind members that
there will be calls for more change. So th e question then becomes: how do we want to
respond to those calls, and how do we expre ss to the public that we do trust them to
acknowledge the right that we have to do our job properly, the right to the tools that we
need to do our job, and the right to fair remuneration for it?
My final comment is that it will always be difficult for us, particularly in terms of
MPs’ pay, for as long as ther e is severe inequity in this  country, for as long as the
minimum wage is a political decision ma de by the Prime Minister and not made
independently of the political environment, a nd for as long as there continues to be an
increase—a significant increase—in higher sala ries, which MPs also receive, and very,
very small incremental increases, if any, in  the lowest wages. That inequity will
continue to bring more scru tiny on MPs. We are making deci sions about other people’s
pay and other people’s employment conditi ons—every year we go through cycles of
making changes to their pay and changes to their employment conditions—and yet we
squeal a little when those decisions are being made about our own pay and employment
conditions. That is not fair, and we will need to change that also. Thank you.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Sat sri akaal, Mr Assistant Speaker.
Thanks for the opportunity to speak on the th ird reading of the Members of Parliament
(Remuneration and Services) Bill. The bill be fore the House for its third reading today
improves the legislation relating to elected members’ remuneration and entitlement to
services. It provides a new framework towa rds providing entitlements for members of
Parliament and the executive. The improvements to the legislation are based on the Law
Commission’s report Review of the Civil List Act 1979: Members of Parliament and
Ministers.
As a member of the Government Admi nistration Committee, I acknowledge the
work that my colleagues, the officials, and the submitters have done on this bill. I agree
with my colleague Chris Auchinvole that this  bill is in line with the Government’s
decision to bring transparency, independence, and non-partisanship into determining the
entitlements of Ministers and members of Parliament.
By way of this legislation, the Rem uneration Authority will decide on the
entitlements of MPs and the executive. Also, under the new legislation, and by way of a
statutory requirement, all MPs, whether present or former, will need to disclose their
travel and accommodation expenses on a pe riodic basis. Furthermore, MPs can no
longer skip Parliament with a token pena lty for their non-attendance. The deduction
from an MP’s salary for non-attendance will rise from $10 a day currently to 0.2 percent
of the member’s salary. This equates to a bout $289 a day. No doubt, this is a significant
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14727
amount to pay, and it will ensure that all of us are present here in the House, doing our
duties. With these words, I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call in the third
reading of the Members of Parliament (Rem uneration and Services ) Bill. It is a good
bill. It has got to be a good bill when, for example, the legislation is based on the
recommendation of the Law Commission in December 2010 that th e current sanctions
for MPs who do not attend Parliament for l ong periods are gros sly inadequate. For
example, when Labour MP Chris Carter  was fined only $10 a day for his 14-day
absence, that was only $140 for that 14-day absence. Under the new law he could be
fined about $289 a day, as my colleague Kanwalj it Singh Bakshi just said, or more than
$4,000. It has got to be a good bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: I commend the Members of Parliament
(Remuneration and Services) Bill to the House.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I will have to write
down that contribution from Jami-Lee Ross after I have finished mine. That was
astonishingly short. I can understand members’  reticence to make a contribution on this
bill, but I think we do owe it to the public to at least discuss the contents of the bill and
discuss what it is designed to  do. It may be something that we as members feel a little
uncomfortable discussing in front of the public , but the fact that it makes us feel a little
uncomfortable discussing it probably ought to be one of the reasons why we do actually
have a proper debate about this Members of Parliament  (Remuneration and Services)
Bill.
The purpose of this bill is to establish a new framework for setting entitlements for
members of Parliament and the executive. It repeals the Civil List Act 1979 and changes
the law regarding the salaries and allowanc es of members of Parliament, the support
services provided for members of Parlia ment, Ministers, a nd certain electoral
candidates, the annuities and other benefits an d privileges for form er Prime Ministers,
and the benefits and privileges for former members of Parliament. Essentially, what that
all means is that it modernises the regi me for giving members of Parliament and
members of the executive the resources and to ols we require to carry out the tasks of
being a member of Parliament and being a representative of the people of New Zealand.
A number of members have said—those w ho have contributed to the debate today—
how these things have changed over time . One reason why the regime for pay and
support services for MPs has changed is a de sire for greater transparency—a desire
expressed both by the public and by members of Parliament. But another reason is
simply the fact that the environment in wh ich members of Parliament operate now and
the expectations of members of Parliament  have changed over the years. There was a
time when members of Parliament did not re ceive resources to open an office in their
electorate. They did not receive resources to  staff offices in their electorates and to
provide services to their c onstituents, although most member s of Parliament did. They
either funded it themselves or relied on vol unteers—often members of their family—to
provide those services to their constituen ts. A decision was made, pleasingly, some
decades ago that that was not adequate and our constituents deserved better service than
that, so resources were provided to members of Parliament in order to provide those
services.
Likewise, with the advent of air travel and other forms of travel it was deemed
appropriate that members of Parliament shoul d not only be able to travel to and from
Wellington to carry out their functions here as  legislators but also be able to travel
around the country to carry out their functions as representatives. This is because we do
not just represent the people of our constituencies—although for those of us who are
electorate members of Parliament it is our primary function, I believe, to represent those
14728 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
constituents—it is also incumbent on us to make sure that we are representing the
interests of people across the country. Most of us hold portfolios of one type or another,
and it is a requirement that we travel around and actually speak to the people working in
those areas so that we actually have a grasp of what is happening at the front line, what
is happening in reality, and we do not ge t stuck in the ivory tower that is the
parliamentary complex.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: Or in Nelson.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Yes—Ms Street suggested Nelson might also be an
ivory tower. So these resources are very much made available to members of Parliament
so that we can provide the services that are expected of us.
Other more recent innovations are the internet and email. I am sure all MPs—just
like probably most other people in New Zeal and, and workers in New Zealand—have a
love-hate relationship with emails. They certainly give constituents far better access to
us. It is certainly much faster—usually—to email your member of Parliament and,
hopefully, get a timely response from them, ra ther than relying on old-fashioned mail.
But that, of course, means that we have to be  resourced in order to provide that service;
we have to be accessible and available to ou r constituents. That, ultimately, is what the
resources side of this is about.
Of course, it is also about ensuring that  members of Parliament are reasonably
recompensed for the work that they do. As Ch ris Hipkins rightly pointed out, I think, it
is about striking a balance and ensuring that someone does not need to be independently
wealthy—they do not need to be  a rich person—in order to enter Parliament, because it
is a House of Representatives. We ought to represent the whol e diversity of our
nation—rich, poor, old, young, ethnic ities of all varieties, ba ckgrounds of all varieties,
careers of all varieties. If we were to ove rly restrict the remune ration of members of
Parliament, that would limit the different ki nds of people who could come into this
