place. Nor should you come to Parliament in or der to become rich. That is not a reason
to seek election and to seek to represen t the people whom you pur port to represent. I
think we have, over the years, come up wi th systems that do strike that balance
appropriately. However, members of Parliame nt are well remunerated when compared
with most people in New Zealand. I think we have to acknowle dge that although we
think it is a fair remuneration, we are amongs t the top income earners in New Zealand.
It is understandable that there is scrutiny and an expectation that we will be absolutely
transparent about what we earn and the way we  use the resources th at are available to
us.
So the key changes in this legislation are around improving transparency, and are
around ensuring that we have  the right matters dealt with by the Remuneration
Authority and the right matters dealt with by the Speaker. Particularly, I think it is
important that members of Parliament acknow ledge that our primary function when the
House is sitting is to be here in the House legislating. That is our job. That is not to say
that there are not good, valid reasons why some of us for some of the time need to be
away from the House, but our primary role is  to pass legislation. That is actually what
we are sent here to do. That is what people elect us to do.
One of the key changes that this legislation allows for is to the penalties for being
away from Parliament without good reason, wi thout the authority of the party whips or
the Speaker, depending on the different regime s for different people, whether they be
independent, small parties, or part of a larger party. It is true that the penalty system that
was in place before really had no impact . There was no incentive to carry out our
primary functions and be here in the H ouse under the old system. The new system
certainly does create an incentive for members of Parliament to be here. With it will
come a new regime where we are now all going to be checked off to make sure that we
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14729
are here in Parliament, to ensure that at leas t at some point in time in the day we make
an appearance here in the debating chamber and/or that we make an appearance at a
select committee, and if we do not do that, th at there is a good explanation for that that
the Speaker or the whips are aware of. I think that does create the right incentives and
that members of the public will appreciate that  that expectation has been built into the
legislation.
I think that this is good legi slation. It strikes the right balance both in terms of the
remuneration of MPs and also placing the co rrect responsibilities with the correct
authorities so that the right decisions are made. It grants members of Parliament the
tools they require to carry out the functions of this role to an adequate level and ensures
that the constituents that we serve get the services that they expect from their members
of Parliament. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I think members have traversed the
Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Bill very well and have articulated
very well the main points. In the spirit of this bill, I do not wish to waste any more
taxpayers’ money by taking up Parliament’s time. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Is this going to be a split call?

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: That is up to Labour. No, I understand that it will not
be. Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Ki a ora. I do not think I
will take my full 10 minutes for this ca ll. What we are discussing are MPs’
remuneration and expenses. I think the importa nt thing to put on the public record is
what an incredible privilege it is for each and every one of us to be able to sit in this
Chamber at the public’s pleasure because of th eir direct democracy and their votes. It is
an incredible privilege, and one that we must remind ourselves of every day. We get
budgets to employ staff and to travel the coun try as part of our work, and a very, very
fair remuneration package. I think it is im portant to remember that each and every one
of those dollars is paid by a New Zealand taxpaye r. It is incredibly critical that we are
reminded of the privilege and reminded that  we are not spending our money; we are
spending the public’s money.
I believe that every single member in this  Parliament has entered this Chamber with
a desire to do what is right for this count ry, to do what is behi nd their vision, and I do
not believe that any MP has come to this Parliament to get wealthy. Obviously, though,
there is a huge discrepancy between the average wage, the median wage, the minimum
wage, and the wage that MPs and Ministers get in New Zealand.
It is right that the public should scrutinis e MPs’ expenses and remuneration. It is
right that the public should question the entitlem ents and the perks. It is also right that
the cartoonists and people at barbecues can po ke a bit of fun at MPs as well, because
what we know is that sunlight  is the best disinfectant. It is important that we have a
public conversation out in the open when it co mes to MPs’ entitlements, remuneration,
and other aspects of our financial accountabi lity. For too long it was held behind closed
doors. MPs were seen to be the ones set ting their own pay rate s, setting their own
entitlements, and setting their own supe rannuation. Obviously, the public was against
that, because it is not right. It goes agains t the principles of appropriate decision
making. Those affected should not be the one s setting the decisions. That is why you
see cartoons of pigs in the trough and the like.
So I am quite proud to say that the Gr een Party for a long time has been the
champion of greater transparency and openne ss when it comes to MPs’ remuneration
and expenses. It was the Gr een Party members who in 20 09 publicly and voluntarily
disclosed our expenses, and then we saw the commendable decision by Speaker
Lockwood Smith to apply that across Parliame nt. We believe in transparency. We have
championed it for a long time, and although the Members of Parliament (Remuneration
14730 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
and Services) Bill is a step in  the right direction, and we w ill be supporting it, we still
think that there is some way to go.
So what we see with this bill are, basi cally, a few minor changes. We are seeing the
so-called Chris Carter clause, clause 14, whic h is increasing the daily penalty rate for
MPs who are not present on the precinct or  doing parliamentary wo rk. We are seeing
changes around the Remuneration Authority’s role. What we did originally see in the
first reading of the bill was that MPs’ travel expenses were also going to be moved from
the Speaker to the Remuneration Authority. That was taken out of the bill. It is
something the Green Party attempted to put  back in through an amendment to the
legislation, but it was not successful.
Just to go through a bit of history, it is not just about the recent allegations from the
New Zealand Herald , and in particular the stagge ringly high number of private
superannuation schemes of the National Party members; this has been an issue for a
long time. It is not just about moats and UK parliamentarians rorting the system there;
this has been an issue for a long time. I take your minds back to some of the
superannuation schemes and travel allowances  that, I believe, led to Metiria Turei
putting a motion some years ago to the Parliamentary Service Commission. That
stimulated, I understand, the Law Commission i nvestigation that is the genesis of this
bill, which we should be passing today. It ha s had some history. It is good to be seeing
progress on it.
A point of debate and controversy th rough the second reading and the Committee
stage of the bill was what should happe n with MPs’ travel and accommodation
expenses. We supported the original inclusio n that it should be an independent body
that decides, because if MPs, through the Speaker of this Parliament, are the ones
deciding the travel and accommodation enti tlements, quite rightfully the public can
question whether MPs are making decisions in their own interests.
It is much more desirable to have an independent authority, such as the
Remuneration Authority, setting this entitlement. I also note that Sir Geoffrey Palmer
said it was incredibly sad that this re commendation from the Law Commission was not
adopted. We put the amendment on Supplementary Order Paper 369 to the Committee.
Unfortunately, it was not successf ul, but I think that this is where we are ultimately
going to see it, because the principle is consistent. Those making decisions and
benefiting from them should not be making those decisions.
I would also like to acknowledge the am endment put up by the member Brendan
Horan on Supplementary Order Paper 368, whic h was to have a 3- year freeze on
remuneration entitlements. I think that from the public’s perspective it is absolutely
galling that they are struggling to pay the power bills, they are struggling to purchase
healthy food, and housing costs are going th rough the roof, but what we see every
Christmas, it seems, is MPs getting another pay rise. Despite their being set by an
independent authority, we also know that those pay rises only ever go in one direction.
So we think having a 3-year freeze could help the public have some more confidence
in it. Obviously, we have now got to a state where there is a media frenzy before every
Christmas about what the pay rise will be fo r MPs and how far it will be backdated. We
support the proposal that it shoul d be set at a 3-year period so we would not be getting
those constant increa ses. So we put up some proposal s and we supported some other
proposals. They did not pass, but ultimately I think this is the start of a process for
greater transparency and openness for our Parliament.
We would like to celebrate the inclusi on of greater support for members with
disabilities. I think Mojo Mathers has made history by being the first deaf MP in our
Parliament. What we saw in the early days of her taking her seat in this House were
some wrangles over who was going to pay for her support. What this legislation does is
14 Nov 2013 Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 14731
say very clearly that every MP has the right to fully participate in the House, and if
additional services are needed, they will be provided, whether they be for a member in
wheelchair, which may mean we have to modify the Chamber and the precincts,
through to providing a TV screen and translatio n services so Mojo can participate fully
in this House. I think it is  critical that this Parliament  sends a message to all New
Zealanders, no matter what thei r disability, that their view s and opinions are respected,
they are valued, and we want to hear them. What we do not want to be doing is sending
the signal, either consciously or subconsciously, exp licitly or implicitly, that disabled
members, because of the extra needs, should feel guilty about taking extra resources.
Thirdly, in this bill we are seeing the a ttendance register for MPs being created in
statute. I know the Standing Orders Committ ee is looking at how we are going to deal
with this in practice. I think what we are goi ng to see is an extra workload for the whips
and the Speaker of Parliament, but I believe what we saw with the member Chris Carter
was that the $10 a day fee was simply laughable. Increasing that figure will give the
public greater confidence. Ultimately, this is what this legislation is all about. It is about
the public being able to have confidence in their elected officials—all of us who have
the privilege to sit in this House—to represent the people of New Zealand. To represent
our electorates and constituencies, we need th em to have confidence. If MPs are seen to
be rorting the system, we are lessening the respect for this institution.
Four quick points I want to say going forwar d are, firstly, obviously we need to set
travel allowances independently. Secondly, I think we need to remove the personal
travel perk. I know it is seen with a great de al of scorn by the public that MPs can go on
a holiday on the taxpayer’s dime  through their travel entitlements. I understand this is a
historical remuneration packag e, but I do not think that the public understands it. I do
not think the public sees the rationale behind it. It is something that I do not use and
have never used. I think in the future this has to go.
Obviously, travel for professional, parliame ntary business, is most appropriate. But
every time you are at the airport—and I am sure that many members have this—most
likely on parliamentary purpose, the public are looking at you, questioning whether you
are off to Great Barrier Island or Queenstown for a weekend. So I think for the public to
have greater confidence in the system this mu st be removed. Thirdly, I think we need to
have greater transparency and increase the ability of the Official Information Act to
include how parties spend their public money.
I think there is a lot more we can do. This is just the beginning. It is not the end. I
think the public and this Pa rliament should celebrate greater openness and transparency
when it comes to financial accountability for our elected members of Parliament. Kia
ora.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: When the member for Palmerston
North spoke a few moments ago he expressed some surprise—and in fact he was quite
critical—at the fact that some of the latter speakers from the National side in this debate
made very short contributions. This is a matter of genuine public inte rest so I just want
to put it on the record for anybody who may be listening that there are actually only two
National MPs on the Government Administra tion Committee who are eligible to speak
in debates in this House. That is actually the reason for that. In fact, I should also point
out, since the chair of the committee, Ruth Dyson, is interjecting at the moment, that not
all the Labour speakers have taken their calls in  this debate either. So I think they just
need to be mindful of the fact that it cuts both ways.
The Government Administration Committee,  nevertheless, has done very good work
on this Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Bill. I was not involved in
their work at all. I did not hear the submi ssions, but by all accounts they did give them
due consideration. They have paid sufficient respect to the sensitivities of the members
14732 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013
of the public on this issue, so I thank them  for that. I acknowledge  the very thoughtful
and intelligent contributions of all members of the House in this third reading debate,
and I too support this bill.
Bill read a third time.

sections.heading: Health And Safety In Employment Amendment Bill

items.text: Third Readings

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I move, That the WorkSafe New
Zealand Bill, the Health and Safety in Em ployment Amendment Bill, and the Mines
Rescue Bill be now read a third time. It gives me great satisfaction to support these bills
at the third readings. Following the releas e of the report of the Royal Commission on
the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy in 2012 this Government committed to implementing
the royal commission’s 16 r ecommendations by the end of  2013. By establishing
WorkSafe New Zealand, strengthening worker participation arrangements in the mining
industry, ensuring that the Mines Rescue service is adequately funded and supported by
legislation, and paving the wa y for a new set of mining hea lth and safety regulations,
these bills fulfil key elements of that commitment.
Both the royal commission and the Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and
Safety recommended that a new regulator be established in the form of a Crown agent.
A stand-alone agency sufficiently resourced and with an executive board with a wide
range of skills and experience will have the necessary focus to help reduce New
Zealand’s high rate of fatalities and serious injuries in the workplace. But just creating a
new agency is not enough on its own. The es tablishment of WorkSafe New Zealand is
just one aspect of the most  significant reforms to the wo rkplace health and safety
system in a generation.
As I announced recently, this Government in tends to introduce a replacement for the
Health and Safety in Employment Act,  which is now over 20 years old. The new
legislation will be supported by a full spectrum of regulations, approved codes of
practice, and other guidance material in support of the primary legislation. This was one
of the areas that drew part icular criticism from the r oyal commission in relation to
mining. The commission identified that ther e was a lack of supporting material sitting
beneath the Health and Safety in Employment Act. So although duty holders knew what
they had to comply with, they had no guidance as to how to comply. In the high-hazard
industry of coalmining, this fact, among others, led to the tragedy at Pike River.
The Health and Safety in Employment Am endment Bill will pave the way for a new
set of mining health and safety regulati ons, as recommended by the royal commission.
These regulations, among other things, will se t out the processes that  must be followed
and the minimum standards that must be me t to safely manage the hazards that can
cause catastrophic failure of the kind seen at Pike River. Mine operators will be required
to develop detailed hazard management plan s to demonstrate how they will meet these
requirements. These regulations will bring the regulation of mining health and safety in
New Zealand into line with international be st practice. I would like to express my
appreciation to both the expert reference gr oup that has been advising officials and the
industry stakeholders who have engaged in a productive and ope n manner throughout
the development of these regulations.
The Health and Safety in Employment Am endment Bill also responds to another
recommendation of the royal commission by significantly strengthening worker
participation arrangements in the mining industry. The provisions of this bill will ensure
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14733
that all mine workers at a mining operation, including contractors, subcontractors, and
labour hire workers, will be covered by these arrangements.
Health and safety representatives will be supported by a range of statutory functions
and powers. Those who have undertaken prescr ibed training will be able to carry out
inspections and suspend operations  if there is an imminent ri sk of serious harm. In the
underground coalmining sector, which has seen the vast majority of  the fatalities in
mining in the last 60 years, these strengthe ned provisions will be further supported by
the appointment of industry h ealth and safety representati ves, who will provide, in the
royal commission’s words, “an extra set of eyes and ears”.
The Mines Rescue Bill responds to the recommendation of the royal commission
concerning the mines rescue service. The bill clearly sets out the functions of the service
and the legislation, and provides that the le vy to fund the service can be set through
regulations. These changes will ensure that th is vital service is sufficiently resourced to
assist mine operators with their emergency preparedness and to respond to emergencies
and other incidents when required.
This bill also provides statutory support for the role of the incident controller in a
major underground mining emergency. This is a key role in the inter-agency protocol
that has been developed in response to another of  the royal commission’s
recommendations. The incident controller will lead the decision making at the mine site
during an emergency. This legislation will ensure that he or she can effectively carry out
this important task.
It is our duty to the 29 workers who di ed, and their families, to oversee the
implementation of the royal commission’s recommendations. It is also a duty we owe to
all current and future workers in the mi ning industry in New Zealand. These bills
implement several key recommendations of  the royal commission and I commend them
to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak on what is now a collection
of three bills—the WorkSafe New Zealand Bi ll, the Health and Safety in Employment
Amendment Bill, and the Mines Rescue Bill—on  this very important topic. Labour has
supported this legislation, notw ithstanding some reservations we have had about it, and
actually continue to have, and I will come to  those shortly. But, as the Minister of
Labour has pointed out, this Health and Sa fety in Employment Amendment Bill makes
some significant changes and I am confident that it will make a significant difference, at
least in the extractive industries that it largely refers to. The introduction of beefed-up
powers for the site health and safety representatives, and the introduction of the new
beast, if you like, th e “industry health and safety repr esentative”, are innovative steps.
They are new steps—some would say long-aw aited steps—but, nevertheless, that is
now happening under the Health and Safety in  Employment Amendment Bill, and they
are both welcome changes.
As I said, this legislation falls short in some areas, and I will comment on those
shortly, but it does provide a foundation on which to build. Labour will await the
introduction of the broader reform of the Health and Safety in Employment Amendment
Bill, which is the bill that is currently the subject of an exposure draft that has gone out
to sector groups and others. Depending on what is in that bill, we will build on some of
the parts of the present legislation, this  Pike River implementation package of
legislation.
Before I go further, I want to make a plea. This legislation corrects some
longstanding flaws and failures in our health and safety legal framework. It no longer
matters which Government over the last 20 years did or did not do the right thing.
Parliament is now fixing it. We are plugging the gaps and we are paving the way for a
safer New Zealand and safer workplaces in New Zealand. But it would be an insult to
14734 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013
deny that we have been brought to this point by the worst and possibly the most
avoidable industrial tragedy in nearly 100 y ears—the most lives lost in an industrial
tragedy, I should say, since the 1914 Huntly mi ne disaster, when 43 men perished. The
truth is that getting this legislation even  this far has seen many New Zealand workers
pay the ultimate price. Twenty-nine of them still lie entombed deep within the Paparoa
Range. By passing this legislation, this Parliament acknowledges the price those 29 men
and their families paid, and by putting asid e our usual fractious and antagonistic
behaviour and accepting that nothing less than meaningful change is necessary, and by
acting accordingly.
But that is not enough. In truth, this Parl iament and successive executives that have
been part of it were part of the failure of the system that led to the tragedy we now know
as Pike River. The Royal Commission on th e Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy found
failure by the company and by the Government as regulator. A court has since found the
company at fault, but then that court ha d only the company before it. The regulator
prosecuted the company but did not prosecute its elf. In July this ye ar Judge Farish of
the District Court in Greymouth imposed on Pi ke River Coal the highest aggregate fine
and reparation order imposed on any employer under the Health and Safety in
Employment Act—$760,000 in fines, and $3,410,000 in reparation. The judge said that
the fines are to condemn the practices of the company and “to indicate that this
company should never have been in operation”.
Mr Bridges, we let that company operate. Mr Key, make good the losses the families
have suffered. Mr Key, accept on behalf of  your Government and all Governments
before it that the Crown failed those wo rkers and failed their families. Make a
contribution. Do something. Put a line under this for the families. Take the final act to
restore the confidence of the families, the fa ith of the people, and the dignity of this
House. Let the Pike 29 rest in peace.
Let me turn to three points in this legislation where improvement is still possible.
They are the three points that we have debated in this House during the passage of this
legislation when it was originally one bill— it is now three bills—as it worked its way
through. The first point is the governing board of WorkSafe New Zealand. The future of
health and safety in this country must be built on a genuine, respectful relationship, both
at a corporate level and at an enterprise level, between workers, their employers, and the
Government—a genuinely tripartite structure and model. That must start at the top, and
the top, when it comes to a regime affec ting health and safety, is WorkSafe New
Zealand, the new body established to champion the cause and regulate workplace health
and safety, and make life safer and better fo r workers in New Zealand. But that should
reflect a genuinely tripart ite model too, and it does not  at the moment. I ask the
Minister, when he gets to a poi nt, at some point, to review the legislation to bear that
point in mind.
The second point is the scope of the ro le of the industry health and safety
representatives under new section 19ZP in the Health and Safety in Employment
Amendment Act, in this package of bills. As it  stands now, that role is confined to only
underground coalmining, but it should apply to tunnelling and quarrying as well. We are
only 2 or 3 weeks out from the aftermath in the District Court in Auckland of a
tunnelling disaster that led to  a fatality and serious injury to people involved. It was not
a mine and it was not a tunnel that was there for extractive purposes—it was there to lay
cables, and it was in an urban area—but ther e was a build-up of gas, which exploded
and killed and maimed. There is no less reason for there to be the best possible health
and safety regime covering that  type of work than there is for underground coalmining.
Indeed, other forms of mining, such as open-cast coalmining, are nevertheless
coalmining activity. It is hazardous and dangerous, and there is as much a case for the
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14735
industry health and safety re presentative in that situati on as there is for underground
coalmining, notwithstanding the extra-sp ecial hazards involved in underground
coalmining, and I ask the Minister to bear that in mind for future consideration.
The third point is—and it seems a somewhat  small point, and hopefully is a situation
that we will never have to experience again— the role of the incident controller in a
significant and large-scale incident such as the one that happened at Pike River. The
way it is defined at the moment, the incident  controller who is appointed by WorkSafe
New Zealand but is required to consult with the range of other agencies that invariably
get involved—the Police, the Fire Service, the Mines Rescue trust—is required to
consult with every other agency, but there is  no signal given in the legislation about the
need for timely and effective decision-maki ng, which was one of th e let-downs in the
early days, the first week or 10 days, of the Pike River incident. They might seem small
issues, but they are important issues.
Let me conclude by congratulating the Mi nister on shepherding this legislation
through. These are big steps taken in the le adership and management of health and
safety in every workpl ace in New Zealand. We look forw ard to the next phase that the
Minister is putting through as well. This w ill be good for New Zealand. It will be good
for miners in the mining industry in New Z ealand and, ultimately, it will be a signal for
us all to be more careful for those who work  in our workplaces and generate the wealth
that keeps this country the great place that it is.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I just want to follow on from the
two speeches we have had first up and pay tribute and our respect to those miners who
were lost in that terrible tragedy. I th ink the Minister of Labour, Simon Bridges,
expressed that very well and Andrew Little also expressed that very well in his speech
just passed. The Transport and Industrial Relations Committee did travel to the region,
and I would like to acknowledge Damien O’Connor, who will probably be speaking
soon, and Chris Auchinvole. Both have a sp ecial interest in that area. I also
acknowledge our Green members as well for thei r work in that event, when we went
down there.
This is not a pretty occasion for any Parliament or any community to have to go
through. It is something that I guess brings  home the dangers that a workplace does
involve. It brings home the danger that many people engage in every day, in trying to
make this country the productive place that it is. It also brings home the role that the
Government, business, and the community have  in protecting and looking after people
who are engaging in work that may involve that kind of level of danger.
As the last speaker said, this legislat ion—the WorkSafe New Zealand Bill, the
Health and Safety in Employment Amendm ent Bill, and the Mines Rescue Bill—is
overdue and is probably something that many parliaments should have done a long time
ago. Unfortunately, that is the s ituation, but this is the nature  of this legislation and the
circumstances we are now in. In saying that, this is good legislation. I would just like to
thank the Minister, Simon Bridges, who has done an excellent job in listening to the
community, being aware of these issues, and trying to find a way to incorporate into
legislation the needs of our communities in a way that is practical and will work going
forward. I also thank the members of the select committee—National, Labour, and the
Greens—who have been part of that committ ee and have worked conscientiously to get
the best result for the community.
When we look at this legislation it does make some significant changes, which have
been canvassed by both speakers, and there have been some changes at the select
committee really just to accommodate some practicalities of different industries,
looking at finding the balance that will be the be st so that we can maintain safety in a
very dangerous mining industry, especia lly where coalmining is involved. It is
14736 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013
underground, and there is the possibility that gas could explode and then cause loss of
life, as we saw at Pike River.
This legislation is a balance in trying to achieve the recommendations of the Royal
Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Trage dy in regard to that situation, but at the
same time being the right balance for busine ss, community, and also employees as they
go about their daily work in ou r best industries. This is le gislation that all political
parties have shown an endeavour to work towards getting through this House, and we
commend it to the House.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : Every time I rise
to speak on the Health and Safety (Pike Ri ver Implementation) Bill and the legislation
arising out of it, there is so much to say. It has been a long time coming to this House. I
have to acknowledge that this is good legisl ation, but it is not perfect. We have pointed
to the deficiencies that we believe are stil l in it, but it is good legislation, necessary
legislation.
It started back in 1992 with the change to the law that, in effect, placed the onus of
safety on to employers and employees, in the belief that they coul d get on and ensure a
safe workplace. I remember warnings to  me personally in 1995 about what might
happen. In 1999 we raised thes e issues in the Government, again to be refuted by
officials, who had the wisdom of experience, they said, a nd knew what was best for all
health and safety but mine safety in partic ular. In the meantime, within the country we
continued to see—and still do, of course, in  some industries—workers killed and not
returning home from their workplaces.
I would like to acknowledge the excellent sp eech from my colleag ue Andrew Little,
who summarised all the issues very, very we ll. I apologise if perhaps I might be less
focused and a bit more emotional relating to issu es that have been part and parcel of the
culture of our West Coast economy for a long time.
The assurances, once again repeated from Wellington, were about concerns that had
been in the community and in the workpl ace for a number of years. There were
assurances from the Minister of Labour as recently as 2010 that employers were in a
good position to understand the hazards arising in their workplaces and were best placed
to take steps to control them. That was not the truth. It was not the reality. This
legislation will make some changes to rebalan ce the input into health and safety in the
workplace, and it is necessary.
There have been a lot of words, a lot h eard, a lot said, and, we hope, a lot learnt
through the process of the royal commission pos t - Pike River. We have a summary. It
is just a small document, wh ich I am holding up, with some of the wisdom that came
from that royal commission. There is a book to be launched in Greymouth tomorrow
that contains a lot more wisdom—a summa ry, a very good summar y, of what happened
down there. That is good. We need to have things written down so that in the future
people can look back and learn fr om the mistakes that have been made, but in the end it
is action that is important. No amount of words, whether they be oral or in written form,
mean enough to ensure safety into the future, without action.
One of the issues that are still to be resolved is the one of accountability. My
colleagues spoke of it. There were assuran ces, and support was given to the families at
the time of the tragedy. They needed that, and it was acknowledged at the time. But
moving beyond the lessons of th e royal commission and into the changes in legislation,
as we have seen here, there has not really been one person held to  account, other than
the previous Minister perhaps, who resigned because she was in the wrong place at the
wrong time. Next year, we believe, there wi ll be a court case here in Wellington, not on
the West Coast, so that that person will be tried not by their peers but actually by
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14737
another group of people outside  the region. I am not going to  get into the wisdom of
that.
There is a reasonable expectation from fam ilies, and they want some accountability.
Accountability comes not just from nice apologies; it actually comes from
acknowledgment of the mistakes made—and it is fairly hard to deny those—followed
by action. The payment to families that has been, I guess, reasonably expected is not for
some kind of mercenary offset for the tragic losses that those families have suffered; it
is the action part of accountability that comes after acknowledgment. There has been
acknowledgment of the mistakes, as I have sa id, and there has been a royal commission
that points to the areas of fault, but there has been no real action.
I implore the Government to actually take action, to make a payment to families as
an acknowledgment of the failings at ever y level of Government responsibility: not
resourcing the mines inspectorate, having in adequate legislati on, not having put in
codes of practice, and not running a system that gave some reasonable expectation of
safety not only at Pike Rive r but, in fact, at Spring Creek Mine as well. The failures
were systemic. They were the responsibility of Governments. I do not think that anyone
can step back from that. But the Government of the day—that is, the National
Government now—has a responsibility to take action, following acknowledgment, to
deliver accountability. Then the families can move on.
The families have some comfort from the changes being made through this
legislation in the House toda y, but there is still reluctan ce. The Prime Minister says
payment to them may set a precedent. I th ink that is rubbish. What kind of precedent
has been laid down by a $30 million paymen t to a huge multinational for no guarantee
of jobs? What precedent is set if you do sweet deals to get economic development in
this country through Skycity? That is a precedent—I say a far more dangerous
precedent than paying something as acknowle dgment and accountability for systemic
Government failure. That is a reasonable reque st. In the passage of this legislation, the
Government has acknowledged that change was needed. It has taken action here, but it
needs to acknowledge that faults were made and to take action by way of some form of
payment to families.
I hope to be at the launch of the book I am holding, Tragedy at Pike River Mine ,
tomorrow. I am working my way through it. It is a factual recollect ion of the very sad
set of circumstances leading up to and through the whole Pike River disaster.
But the next chapter is not written. That w ill be what has come from this. I hope that
it is written in 10 years’ time. I hope that th e Minister can rightfully claim that he has
done his part to make the necessary change s in health and safety in mining, but he
knows full well that, actually, the resources to en sure that that occurs have not been put
in place. The fact that we ha d two mine inspectors when the Pike River mine blew up
and we now have three, with one head inspec tor, does give an indication that there is
still much to be done in this area and that there are resources to be put in place. The
establishment of WorkSafe New Zealand is a step forward, the ability of workers to
have input into workplace health and safety  is a step forward, and the upgrade of the
Mines Rescue Trust Act is a step forward, but  they are only steps. We need action,
delivery of the necessary resources, and commitment from the Government to be
accountable for the terrible mi stakes that have occurred through Governments and that
led to this disaster.
My final plea in the passage of this legi slation is to say follow through, Minister.
Talk to your leader, John Key. He comforte d the families at the time. He needs to
comfort the families now, show accountability, and, with the Government, acknowledge
the terrible losses that they have suffered.
14738 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Next Tuesday will mark the third anniversary of the Pike
River disaster and I wanted to begin this contribution by reading a couple of paragraphs
from the summary of the report of the R oyal Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine
Tragedy. “It is the commission’s view that  even though the company was operating in a
known high-hazard industry, the board of director s did not ensure that health and safety
was being properly managed and the executive managers did not properly assess the
health and safety risks that the worker s were facing. In the drive towards coal
production the directors and executive managers paid insufficient attention to health and
safety and exposed the company’s workers to unacceptable risks. Mining should have
stopped until the risks could be properly managed. The Department of Labour did not
have the focus, capacity or strategies to  ensure that Pike was meeting its legal
responsibilities under health a nd safety laws. The department assumed that Pike was
complying with the law, even though there was ample evidence to  the contrary. The
department should have prohibited Pike from  operating the mine until its health and
safety systems were adequate.” The commi ssion goes on in damni ng quote after quote,
saying that the law was inadequate, and de scribing our own regul atory framework as
being years behind those in operation in similar countries.
The fact is that those 29 men were funda mentally and comprehensively betrayed and
let down by the directors of the company, who drove increased production at all costs
yet dealt with health and sa fety as a tick-box exercise, and by the Pike River Coal
management, for its failure to implement proper policies and procedures, and its failure
to implement training, ignoring health and safety advice, an d taking short cuts at every
turn. Those men were let down by the mi nes inspectors, w hose monitoring and
enforcement were totally inadequate. They were let down by the senior management of
the Department of Labour who under-resour ced those same mines inspectors and
ignored the pleas for further resourcing. It also applied a light-handed approach to
regulation of the mining industry. They were let down by Bill Birch, Max Bradford, and
all of those in this House w ho voted for those laws to gut health and safety regulation
and to gut the mines inspector ate, and all the subsequent Parliaments that, as Andrew
Little says, have failed to reverse those until now.
We come now to putting right. The royal commission and the Independent Taskforce
on Workplace Health and Safety have certainly  done their jobs. The question, as I said
in my second reading contribu tion, is whether we in this  House have done our jobs. I
still have a question mark over that matte r. Chris Finlayson, to his great credit,
acknowledged in this House the role that deregulation had played in creating the
environment that caused this disaster. But on the same day John Key denied that same
role. Simon Bridges is the ne w Minister of Labour. I have not yet heard the Minister
speak about the matter of deregulation and what role it played. So for me the jury is out
as to whether the Government acknowledges th at deregulation of h ealth and safety and
deregulation of the mining industry played that  crucial role in creating the environment
that created the disaster.
The fact is that this G overnment still comes from that same DNA of that 1990s
Government. The Government still sees its ro le as facilitating business and maximising
its profits, and sees people as just the labour  input into the microeconomic theory of the
firm. I believe that that is inadequate. So, despite all the assurances of implementing the
royal commission’s recommendations, as others  have said, for me, these bills arising
from the Health and Safety (Pike River Im plementation) Bill are still inadequate.
Andrew Little has spoken of se veral of the matters that he has repeatedly raised and I
also have repeatedly raised in the House.
The creation of WorkSafe is the right thing to do, but the Government still steps back
from a genuine commitment to tripartite regu lation of health and safety. That board of
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14739
WorkSafe will still be accountable to the Mi nister and not to workers or to employers.
That is wrong. In my view, the functions of  the organisation are st ill inadequate. They
actually describe the light-hande d approach to ensuring hea lth and safety that I have
mentioned already in this contribution. And the failure of the Government to
comprehend that this is not  just about underground coalmi ning seems to me to be a
failure of responsibility and a failure to understand one of the basic findings of the royal
commission. So, yes, as other speakers have said, this is a really major step forward, but
it is also a lost opportunity and I regret that. If the Minister disagrees, I say to him now:
“Show me. Show me, show the families of  the 29, and show my community that,
actually, you are genuine about this health and safety business.”
The Green Party is voting for this legislati on, but we regret that it is not better
legislation. Those failures that I have men tioned—to act ethically and responsibly to
prevent this disaster from occurring—are now being mirrored, as my colleague Damien
O’Connor has said, in the failure to take re sponsibility for putting things right. Peter
Whittall is still to face charges, but others  who are implicated in this business have
escaped accountability. The owners  of Pike River Coal have  not been held accountable
and have not stepped up to fund the settleme nts that the court has awarded the families
of the 29. They were happy to take the profits and happy to own that mine, but not
happy to actually fund the consequence of th eir company acting illegally. The directors
who made the decisions around the short cuts likewise have gotten away scot-free from
accountability for this disast er and for the loss of those 29, and despite their own
personal wealth have also declined to actually fund compensation to those families.
The Department of Labour, which investigat ed Pike River Coal, did not even bother
to investigate its own inacti on—one of its statutory responsib ilities. It did not bother to
investigate whether or not charges against its elf were appropriate. So that department
also escapes scot-free, and with the Prim e Minister’s announcements this week, the
Government, which the Department of Labour represented, is also declining to fund any
kind of compensation for the failure of its de partment to perform its duties properly. It
seems as though those who actually take a loss from this are the 29  families and the 29
men who still lie underground at the Pike River mine.
In preparing this contribution I opened the front of the royal commission report,
where the photographs of the 29 men and boys are a constant reminder to me. I live in
Greymouth. I knew quite a number of these men. Joseph Dunbar of ten played league
with my nephew. I often intera cted with that boy. I cannot he lp but feel that this House
has not met its responsibilities, and I expre ss my regret to my community and those
families that we have not been able to live up to the debt that we owe them.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Could I make just a short contribution. I
just want to acknowledge a few people—firs tly, and obviously, the Minister of Labour
and the work he has done on this legislatio n arising from the Health and Safety (Pike
River Implementation) Bill. He has done a heck of a lot of work across this labour space
around health and safety and workplace safety—and still a lot more to come. I just want
to also acknowledge three pa rticular members of the Tran sport and Industrial Relations
Committee, all members who have contribute d to this legislation—they are Damien
O’Connor, Chris Auchinvole, and, of course, the member who has just resumed his seat,
Kevin Hague, for his heartfelt contribution. I just want to acknowledge all three and say
that as someone who has little knowledge or  experience in this area and who does not
come from the area, I think you have abso lutely represented your constituents, your
experience, and those views very, very well.  I do not necessarily agree with all the
views that were shared, but I certainly respect all of those members for their
contributions to this legislation.
14740 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013
The genesis of this is a tragic event a nd we have reflected well on that—and so we
should. But I think, for me, the important th ing in acknowledging the mistakes and the
oversights, looking back through a lens with  20/20 hindsight, is to  ensure that the
balance is achieved so that th e pendulum is not seen to sw ing too far, because in every
matter of health and safety there are two elem ents to it, really. Those elements are the
systems and the processes that we have in place, and obviously this place has a role to
play in the legislative framework that assist s and establishes the right platform for that.
But there is also the human element. Th e human element is one that cannot be
underestimated in terms of the role that each individual must have in using their
common sense, their work experience, thei r training, and their compassion, care, and
understanding of the environment they are wo rking in and of the colleagues they are
working with, as to the role that each indivi dual must play in terms of health and safety.
Although there are some legislative levers that we can pull in terms of ensuring
compliance with legislation, we can never escape th e fact that every individual in every
workplace has a role and a responsibility to think and act and work in a safe manner,
and we must support them to do that.
But when we go too far in terms of swinging that pendulum so that that role and that
responsibility, the personal responsibility fo r the individual, are somehow taken away
and replaced by some system or some le ver or consequence, or so forth, it can
sometimes result in people defaulting to the system and forgetting about themselves. I
am in no way suggesting that that is the cas e in terms of the Pike River disaster or
anything that is linked to this legislation. I make it simply as a point, as a balance in
legislation, that we should al ways remember that it is a match between the systems, the
processes, the levers that we put in place, and the individual human s who contribute to
working them, if you like.
I want to just reiterate that this legisla tion does create three, effectively, new streams
or levers. It creates WorkSafe New Zeala nd, a new regulatory regi me that puts clear
expectations on hazard management and ev erything that falls unde rneath that, and, of
course, the new Mines Rescue Act. As to  the importance of them, I think Damien
O’Connor has rightly pointed out the importance of the skill sets th at come with those
who are involved in this pa rticular industry of undergr ound mining, and the difficulties
and challenges that it brings.
Again, I just want to commend those members for the contribution that they made to
the passage of this legislation. Although we do not agree on everything, actually what
we have done is get good legislation that I hope can help give effect to making the New
Zealand workplace, in particular in the mining area, a safer one.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I stand today on behalf of New Zealand First
to support the third readings of the legislati on arising from the Health and Safety (Pike
River Implementation) Bill. I must quote fr om the New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research report from the Ministry of Busi ness, Innovation and Employment. This sums
up the situation regarding work very well, we believe. It states: “New Zealanders expect
work place safety conditions to be of a standa rd that controls the risk of accidents. In
industries such as mining, maintaining safety  standards are especi ally important since
the environment and operating conditions present a complex range of hazards. These
range from occupational safety hazards th at impact on individua l workers through to
catastrophic accidents that result in multiple injuries and fatalities, as well as economic,
financial, social, and envir onmental damage.” I would like to add to that “the human
loss of life, which is catastrophic.”
We welcome the decision to split this impor tant piece of legislation into three
separate bills. This is a move that actua lly acknowledges that the Pike River mine
tragedy was not caused by a single transgression but by a multitude of factors, all of
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14741
which require attention. It is a move that will allow for each of these very important
sections to get the attention that is needed to implement changes with the level of detail
that is required. In some ways it is an ac knowledgment of the mistakes and the need to
take some action. Like others in this Hous e, we would have liked  to see more firm
action, but this is a start. Although none of these bills will  make up for the Pike River
tragedy, we hope that the families and friends  of those lost are able to take some
comfort in seeing some action taken to preven t future occurrences and minimise danger
in the future.
This legislation is long over due. It is, essentially, practic al and it makes significant
changes. It is very necessary legislation. The WorkSafe New Zealand Bill is setting up
the centralised agency, and, as we have said, this is l ong overdue. This agency needs to
take a strong leadership role in order to protect our worker s in New Zealand. We
applaud the amendments made by the Tran sport and Industrial Relations Committee,
which ensure a sole Government agency that  will have centralised responsibility. This
will lead to responsible health and safety practices being undertaken. But, like previous
speakers, we believe that the board must be a tripartite model. The board cannot afford
to be party political, with members changing after every election.
We are pleased to hear from the Minister of Labour that WorkSafe New Zealand will
have the necessary resources to carry out its functions and to ensure that these
objectives are met. That is absolutely para mount. We hope too that these functions will
be monitored, that the objectives are met, and that if this organisation is not meeting the
requirements, some action is taken. We cannot afford to just sit back on our hands. This
is an area that does need to be followed up.
The Health and Safety in Employment Amendment Bill is a positive step forward,
too, towards the goal of reducing workplace injury and death by 25 percent by 2020.
The Mines Rescue Bill is another very impor tant piece of legisl ation. We know that
underground coalmining has its un ique risks, but the bottom line is that all mining, all
tunnelling, and all quarrying is hazardous, if not dangerous.
New Zealand’s health and safety record is  very poor compared with that of other
countries, particularly when we read the report of the Royal Commission on the Pike
River Coal Mine Tragedy. What  makes our appalling safety record worse is that quite
often we do not learn from mistakes that ha ve occurred in the past. We want to see
changes. Every worker has the right to go home at the end of their working day
uninjured and able to carry on and come back to work the next day. We cannot afford to
ignore advice that would safe lives. New Zeal and First hopes that this legislation will
change that. The Mines Rescue Bill ensures that the Mines Rescue Trust is able and
ready to respond to any future mining emergencies. We cannot have a repeat of what we
saw with Pike River.
In closing, I would like to thank the pe ople who worked on the royal commission’s
report and the members of the Transport a nd Industrial Relations Committee. The final
legislation that is presented here today refl ects the hard work and the commitment that
have gone into ensuring that we have legisl ation that is going to make a significant
difference to our mining sector. We want, and need, that difference. This legislation will
be good for mining in New Zealand and for workplaces in general.
I would like to once again pay our respects to the families and the friends who lost
loved ones in the Pike Rive r tragedy. New Zealand First supports the passing of this
legislation, which we believe is a much-needed step toward s recognising the health and
safety needs within this industry.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to follow Barbara Stewart in
this debate and all the othe r speakers who have been invo lved, because th is is very
much a matter for the whole House to agr ee on, to consider, and to work with. The
14742 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013
tragedy that occurred happened at the time when I was the local electoral MP, and when

We have a large number of memorials thr oughout the West Coast to the 29 miners
who were lost. I honestly feel that what we are creating here is more than an enduring

purpose that everybody who has been involved in  this tragedy would approve of. It was

committee, and the response of the committee wa s a tribute to the way that Parliament

I could speak at length, but there is little purpose to th at, other than to acknowledge

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I want to start by acknowledging the members of
Parliament who have been directly invol ved in this tragedy:  Kevin Hague, Chris
Auchinvole, Damien O’Connor, and, of course, Andrew Little, who was the secretary of
the Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union (EPMU) at the time,
and I think something like 17 of the 29 men were members of his union. Next week,
next Tuesday, is the third anni versary of this dreadful even t, that dreadful day that I do
not think those of us will ever forget. It was a dreadful day when we realised that the 29
men were all dead, that they had all died, th at there was no hope, a nd that they had lost
their lives in a mine in the South Island.
How far we have come in 3 years—how far we have come. I have vivid memories of
the memorial service that many of us went down to. There were 10,000-odd people who
turned up to the memorial service at the racecourse in Greymouth. I remember very well
Peter Whittall speaking at that memorial service. The fellow workers of the dead miners
and the EPMU were down among the crowd, unacknowledged. The union was
unacknowledged, as if it played no part and as if it had no role to play in that workplace.
I also remember very clearly that Peter Whittall was nominated as New Zealander of the
Year. He was treated like a hero—he was treated like a hero.
When you think about Joseph Dunbar, that 17- year-old boy on his first day at work
at the Pike River mine, who actually aske d to go to work on Friday instead of on
Monday because he was so excited about  his job, and when you think about the
responsibilities of people like Peter Whitta ll, it just shows you how much we have,
through the process of the Royal Commissi on on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy,
owned up to some of the things that went wrong and accepted that there is a legacy of
terrible, terrible errors. It shows you how far we have come when we have this
legislation—the WorkSafe New Zealand Bill , the Health and Safety in Employment
Amendment Bill, and the Mines Rescue Bill
I think an important thing to note in this  legislation are the obs ervations of not only
the royal commission but also of the Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14743
Safety that the failure that culminated at the Pike River mine, which occurs in our
workplaces almost every week when a worker  dies, has been driven by labour market
and health and safety deregulation going back 20 years or more. Although we all like to
say New Zealanders should have the right to go to work and come home safely, we have
ignored the role of regulation in making sure that happens. In the Health and Safety in
Employment Act 1992 and the collapse of th e responsibility of the Department of
Labour and the regulator, we have been responsible for negligence.
Although I celebrate this legi slation—with reservations, of course—I still do not
believe, as I have said many times, that  the Minister of Labour understands the
connection between regulation, workers’ rights  and the way they are treated at work,
and health and safety on the job. There is a huge disconnect between  the regulation we
are making in this legislation and the cha nges to the Employment Relations Act he is
pushing through. I suspect that in time—well, maybe we will not have to, because
Labour will repeal those changes, but I hope in time we will not be standing here saying
that that deregulation contributed to more tragedy like this.
I also know that the pain of the families is  far from over. I mean, how does a family
ever get over losing a love d one—a 17-year-old son, a hu sband, a partner? I do not
know how that happens. I hope that this legisl ation will be seen by them as a legacy—a
positive legacy, a meaningful legacy—that offers some comfort to them.
There continue to be many unresolved injust ices. Kevin Hague talked about the lack
of accountability and the fact that no one —no Government agency, individual, or
corporation—has been held to account for the deaths of 29 men. It is very
disappointing, coming up to the third anniversary, to have a Government that is denying
accountability as well, as evidenced by its refusal to entertain the idea of paying
compensation in place of the company, which has refused or been unable to pay these
families out.
I think we need to remember that this tragedy started and ended with systemic
failures by the regulator and by multiple Government departments. The licence should
never have been let to open the mine in the first place. We then had the failure of the
Department of Labour and the running-down of the mines inspectorate so that there
were only two inspectors for the whole mines inspectorate. We had the terrible stories
about how they had to scratch around for res ources and even had to beg for travel so
they could go and inspect mines. That is sy stemic failure, negligence, and not taking
responsibility. For the Government to take no responsibility for the regulator, for its
own Government departments, by offering these families some compensation I find
really abhorrent. Let us not forget that two of the shareholders in the Pike River coal
mine were also Crown agencies. I am talking about ACC and the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund. We all know that ACC has a huge, bulging surplus at the
moment. Why can the Prime Mi nister not pick up the phone  and say “How about it?
How about we help these families put to bed their pain?”
It is true that some of them will have had some small amounts of compensation.
Many of them did not receive ACC, because the men who died did not have dependants.
There were not, of course, any funerals, so there was no ACC assistance with that. They
have had to fork out for travel and for representation. It was not until some weeks—2 or
3 weeks—after the travel that the families we re calling out for someone to help them. I
know that not only has it cost them in bearing the loss that they bear but also it has cost
them financially.
As I said, I hope the passing of this legi slation will offer some comfort to the
families. My colleagues Andrew Little and Kevin Hague have referred to the concerns
we still have about this legi slation and the things that ha ve been missed or that could
have been strengthened. I also hope that when we see the next health and safety bill the
14744 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013
Minister listens and picks up those issues, b ecause we all have a responsibility to make
sure that we never see a tragedy like this  again in New Zealand. The Government has a
responsibility to help those families through th is, and also to make sure that the new
WorkSafe agency is properly resourced. I understand there are now four mines
inspectors. I want to know whether that  is adequate. The Government has a
responsibility to make this work. It is fine to pass legislation but you have got to put the
money in and you have got to make sure it ha ppens. Labour is very pleased to support
this legislation, with, as I said, some reservations. Tha nk you for the opportunity to
speak to it.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It was a harrowing and poignant experience serving
on the Transport and Industr ial Relations Committee and hearing submissions on the
former Health and Safety (Pike River Impl ementation) Bill. As we have heard, two
members of our committee, Kevin Hague a nd Chris Auchinvole, personally knew men
who lost their lives in the Pike River disa ster. It made our c onsideration of this
legislation very personal, and we could share the very real pain of their loss through
their close proximity to us when we were considering the submissions. This legislation
had its genesis in tragedy. It is the earnes t wish of all of us on the select committee—
and I am sure of all of us in this Hous e—that, through the provisi ons contained within
this legislation, future tragedies may be averted.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I rise to speak to the third reading of the legislation
arising from the Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill. The right to go to
work, leave your loved ones in the morning, and come home safe and unharmed at night
is a pretty basic right, and in this instance that right was not upheld. Those 29 men left
in the morning and they never returned. They may never return from where they
currently are. This legislation is one chapter in the book of things that we need to learn
from this disaster. Labour is supporting the th ird reading of this le gislation because this
is part of what we have learnt from this  tragedy. In a previous decade it was Cave
Creek. It seems that pretty much every d ecade in this country we need to remind
ourselves about the importance of workplace rights. It seems that about every decade we
need to go through the misery and the tragedy and relearn lessons that we have learnt
before. I hope that this is the last decade wh en we will have to revisit these types of
remedies.
Some people might think it is the first time th at some of the things contained in this
legislation have ever been contemplated, but, actually, if you look back through history,
some of these are things that we once had and that were stripped away in the name of
deregulation, in the name of having the ma rket—the invisible hand of the market was
going to fix everything. If there is one thing that I can say du ring this debate that I hope
will resonate in this debating chamber for all th e years that it needs to, it is to ask that
we please never have to learn the lesson ag ain. Can we please never have to learn the
lesson again through losing lives. The market and deregulation do not keep people safe
at work—they do not keep peopl e safe. Regulation is an im portant factor in having
civilised, decent workplaces where people can actually have the expectation of the basic
right to earn a living and not to die from it—the basic right to earn a living and not to
die from it.
There are some inadequacies in this legisl ation. We would have much preferred that
all of the recommendations from the Roya l Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine
Tragedy be followed, but they have not. I ge nuinely hope that I or other MPs in the
future will not be back to stand up and revisit that in the future. When the Government
has inquiries of any nature, it would be useful that it picks up all of the
recommendations and does not cherry-pick recommendations. I think that that is
another disaster waiting to happen. When  Governments do not actually look at the
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14745
whole picture and just cherry-pick pieces that  they feel comfortable with, then we are
doomed to fail yet again.
I also want to echo the words of my colleague Darien Fenton and urge the
Government to not believe that it has fixed the problem because of the passing of this
legislation this afternoon. This is but one chapter of what needs to happen. The broader
context is actually having people valued, th eir voices valued, thei r work valued, and
their workplaces valued, and not taking the approach—as the Government has done in
other pieces of legislation—of stripping away workers’ rights. That is the context in
which this series of bills needs to sit. I think that the Governme nt does need to stop,
pause, and think about the broader context of  what constitutes a decent, fair, and safe
workplace.
The last thing that I will do in the course of this debate  is acknowledge the loss that
the families have endured and encourage the Government to make good for those
families. They are still suffering. They will c ontinue to suffer for a very long time. This
is but one chapter. I am pleased that Parlia ment is today making this move, but there is
so much more to do in honouring those men, their families, and the tragedy that has
taken place.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker. T ēnā
koutou e te Whare P āremata. I too am proud to stand here  and take a small role in this
issue. I will start by acknowledging the MPs of the West Coast, the families of the West
Coast, the people who put work into trying to  make this legislation arising from the
Health and Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill better legislation, and all the effort
of the Transport and Industrial  Relations Committee. I would also like to start with a
quote from my own community, Waihī, which could equally be from Pike River. It is an
old quote: “If blood be the price of your cursed wea lth, good God, we have bought it
fair.” That quote from the 1900s  is a sad reminder that health  and safety in the mining
industry have followed trage dy and disaster, rather than  existing beforehand, over and
over and over again. Once again, at Pike Ri ver, coal production, Government inaction,
and deregulation led to the deaths of 29 people who did not need to die.
The mining industry is littered with avoidabl e deaths, as is the forestry industry and
others at this point in time. I do commend th e previous speakers who pointed out that
the environment of deregulation is an environment that can equate to death.
Deregulation in the workplace can  lead to death. So we have to be very serious about
what we are doing in this H ouse right now, and very seriou s about whether these bills
meet the needs of that environment, because we have gone so far away from safe
working environments, based on strong organised labour, for whom the employer has a
good relationship, based on rec ognising that production does not come first over health
and safety. Health and safety should come above production. It is very saddening to see
once again that we are writing pretty good but  not perfect legislation and making steps
forward after the event.
The two things that I want to talk about  are the after-the-ev ent nature of this
legislation and also the nature of truth, reconciliation, and that relationship with
resources, which others have touched upon. In the history of mining the failure to listen
to people who have tried to blow the whistle has led to disasters like this over and over
and over again. As Kevin Hague so clearly said, it is time to put this right. We are
pleased to support these three bills, and this  one is well overdue, but  it is with great
sadness that we remark on the price paid. I ndeed, we want to support other members’
calls for proper compensation. The reason that  we support that call is that truth and
reconciliation, acknowledgment, accountability, and apology do not add up to peace of
mind for those who have been harmed wit hout resources. We see in many processes
around the world that words are beautiful thin gs and apologies can be accepted, but if
14746 Mines Rescue Bill 14 Nov 2013
there is no resource to back those words, and if there is no acknowledgment that the cost
is not only human but financial and real for those people, then we cannot have peace.
It was very disturbing today to hear the first item on the news when I woke up, which
was that Cabinet had decided that no compensation would be  paid to the Pike River
families, because of precedent. It was ve ry disturbing when you think about the South
Canterbury Finance $1.6 billion payout and other interesting payouts that have not been
treated as precedent, but the Pike River families will not get compensation. This is
alongside the comments of Andrew Knight of New Zealand Oil and Gas that there
would be no more payout to the Pike River families. The Green Party says that truth and
reconciliation are necessary, and good law, but that there also needs to be resources to
acknowledge these people.
Others have commented on some of the problems with the legislation, although we
support the good work and its good intent. But we  do feel that some of the issues that
Andrew Little raised around th e incident controller consul ting but with no time frames,
and issues around the tripartite model and the need for union workers with a
background in understanding these issues to be  part of the picture, and the need for
adequate numbers of mines inspectors to be part of the picture, because this is not a trust
board like any other. We need trust not tr ust boards. We need proper representative
involvement in workplace safety, and ther e is expertise across the workforce in
workplace safety.
I would just like to say as a final comment—

SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): I am pleased to take what I believe is
