14 Nov 2013 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14747
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I move, That the
Harmful Digital Communications Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Justice
and Electoral Committee to consider the bill. Rapid advances in technology over the last
few decades have changed the way that pe ople communicate with each other. We now
communicate with, form relationships with, and do business with people on the other
side of the world. Our lives are increasingly entwined in the digital world. Smartphones,
tablets, laptops, and desktop computers are everywhere. Smartwatches are also on the
horizon. Modern technology has opened up a whole new world of opportunities.
However, new technologies also present new challenges. It is now easier than ever to
threaten others, spread destructive ru mours, publish invasive and distressing
photographs, and harass people. People are bullied more easily, instantly, and
anonymously. Bullying is no longer confined to  the classroom or the playground in the
lives of young people. A digita l age has meant that tormentors can harass their target
anywhere, at any time, and the trails of abus e remain in cyberspace for ever. Research
suggests that as many as one in 10 New Z ealanders has personal experience of harmful
communications on the internet. In 2007 it was estimated that one in five adolescents
experienced some form of cyber-bullying or harassment that year.
The Law Commission was asked in May 2012 to fast track its consideration of harm
from digital communications. In August 2012 it made its recommendations on how to
tackle the problem. I want to thank the Law Commission for its thorough work. The bill
will give effect to the commission’s legi slative recommendations. I say “legislative”
because there is already a lot of good wo rk going on to help combat the problems
presented by harmful digital communications . For example, NetSafe is helping people
to deal with these issues by providing users with the tools to protect themselves online.
Schools are also moving to implement policies to deal with cyber-bullying. As the Law
Commission notes, all of these are good m easures, but are simply not enough by
themselves to tackle the problem.
The Harmful Digital Communications Bill  provides for quick , effective, and
proportionate responses to the harm caused by digital communications. The bill sets out
10 communication principles to guide the work  of the approved agency for the courts.
For example, “a digital communication shoul d not be threateni ng, intimidating, or
menacing.” Let me be clear that this bill is not aimed at censoring debates and robust
exchanges of ideas, or suppressing speech onlin e. Freedom of speech is something this
Government and all New Zealanders value. Ho wever, free speech is not an absolute
right. It must be balanced with other rights and freedoms. The bill strikes the
appropriate balance between freedom of speech and protecting people from being
bullied or victimised. It also requires the agen cy and the courts to act consistently with
the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act to avoid any doubt about the importance of our
fundamental rights.
The first port of call for complaints about harmful digital communications will be the
approved agency, which will he lp other people to  resolve disputes through negotiation,
through mediation, and by providing advice. Th e majority of complaints should be
resolved by the approved agency without any further need for action. This Government
does not want people unnecessarily involved in the court system, especially our young
people, who may be the victims or the perpetrators of harmful digital communications.
However, for instances where the approved agency cannot resolve the complaint, a
person can apply to the court fo r a number of civil orders. For example, the court could
order a person to remove harmful content, i ssue cease and desist or ders, or reveal the
14748 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14 Nov 2013
identity of an anonymous bul ly. The court will provide sp eedy, informal, and fair
remedies, but will not be able to order fi nes or imprisonment. The most serious cases
can be dealt with through the new criminal  offences of posting a digital communication
with intent to cause harm, punishable by 3 months’ imprisonment; or inciting a person
to commit suicide, punishable by 3 years’ imprisonment. To complement this new
regime there are also amendments to existing law to ensure that they are fit for purpose
and applicable online. For example, the Ha rassment Act is amended so that making
contact online is explicitly included as an action that may constitute harassment.
The final part of the bill that I would lik e to discuss is the safe harbour provision.
This provision clarifies the law relating to websites and other content hosts, and
provides people with an easy, acc essible, and direct way to remove harmful content. A
content host could be any num ber of people—blog sites or organisations, including the
likes of Facebook, Twitter, Vodafone, and TradeMe. Most of our legislation was written
before the advent of the inte rnet and is not always clear about when a content host is
liable for the contents posted by its users. Some recent court decisions suggested that
the content host could be liab le for unlawful content that they do not even know about.
Given the ease and speed of posting cont ent online and the volumes of information
involved, the majority of conten t hosts cannot actually read and vet all content before it
is published.
The safe harbour operates via a notice a nd take-down regime. Broadly speaking, an
online content host will not be liable for unlawful content that another person has posted
on the website unless they are notified that the content is unlawful and fail to take
reasonable steps to remove the content. The basic principles behind this safe harbour
are, as with the rest of the bill, personal responsibility and fairness. The author of a
harmful or illegal communication should be re sponsible for it. Content hosts should not
be liable for things they have no knowledge of.
This bill is not a silver bullet. It will  not stop overnight people bullying and posting
harmful content online. It will, however, cr eate a First World regime to complement
other efforts already taking place to effectively tackle harmful digital communications. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I rise to talk on this new bill, the Harmful Digital
Communications Bill, and to indicate that the Labour Party will support the bill going to
the Justice and Electoral Committee for closer examination.
It is fair to say that this bill is yet anot her step in the struggle for the law and for
Parliament to catch up with, and make some  order out of, the anarchic world of the
internet and social media. The objectives of the bill are, needless to say, laudable. They
are about mitigating harm. We have seen, in a very extreme example in just the last
couple of weeks, how social media, at leas t, can be used to be humiliating and abusive
to people who may not have known originally that they were being treated in that sort of
way.
I have to say that the objective of the bill that says that it is about providing a quick
and efficient means of redress looks more cynical when you see that it means that
redress is to be obtained by private action—private civil action—in the District Court. It
is cynical because it is then left up to the victim—or the putative victim—to have to
meet the cost of going to court to apply for an order, whether it is an interim order to get
material taken down or a longstanding or permanent order that is slightly more punitive.
Nevertheless, it is the victim who has to meet that cost. There would not be many
people, I suggest, who are acti ve on social media today an d who are frequent users of
the internet—let us call them the digita l natives—who have the means to instruct
counsel and go to court for these sorts of things.
14 Nov 2013 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14749
Of course, the other reason for my cynicism  is that the District Court is already
overloaded and there are long delays in many courts. So there is a real question about
whether it has the capacity to pick up an ex tra load of work, given the growing numbers
of people who are active daily on the internet and on social media.
Another issue that we will be examining closely when this goes to the select
committee is that one of the faults of this bi ll, in our view, is the same as the fault in
others being sponsored by the same Minist er—not the Associate Minister who just
spoke, Chester Borrows, but the Minister of  Justice, Judith Collins. Let me draw a
comparison with the Victims’ Orders Agains t Violent Offenders Bill. That, again, is
dependent on civil action. The victim has to meet the cost of dealing with something
that, actually, the criminal justice system a nd the State might be better equipped to deal
with. The harmed person has to go to the Di strict Court. They have to go at their
expense. Under the modern legal aid regime  there is real doubt about whether they
would qualify for legal aid, and even if they do, they may well be subject to the
requirement to repay it, and that repayment is then subject to interest. This is not
looking good for the people who are most likely to be victims of abuse on the internet
and therefore the people who are needing to av ail themselves of this legislation. So we
will be asking, if it is to re main in a civil jurisdiction, whether some easily accessible
means can be made available to ensure that people can actually partake of the provisions
in this bill.
Just turning to some of the issues of substance in the bill, and I do not want to get too
heavily into this, as it is yet to be examin ed by the select committee, but we will be
looking also at the communication principl es. Chester Borrows spoke about one of
them. I note that principle 2 in clause 6 says that “A digital communication should not
be threatening, intimidating, or menacing.” So  it will be interesting to compare, for
example, the Minister of Justice’s own tw eets over the last several months under that
provision to see just how comp liant they are. Then we migh t even look not just at the
Minister of Justice’s tweets but at her good friend Cameron Slater’s contributions on the
internet to see the extent to which they comply with these communication principles.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Very abusive.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Well, principle 3 says: “A digital communication should not
be grossly offensive to a reasonable person in the complainant’s position.”

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: That’s Whale Oil gone.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Well, every time Whale Oil takes a breath, of course, he is in
breach of that provision. But the question there is, of course, that I think lawyers will be
having a field day with what is “a reasona ble person in the complainant’s position.”
That looks like a shifting test , and the courts will be having  great difficulty with it. So
no doubt, with the assistance of the erstwhile Scott Simpson, there will be considerable
consideration given to this as Mr Simps on shepherds the bill through the committee. I
know that he will be wanting to make sure, for the sake of his own reputation, that a
good quality piece of legislation comes out of  the sausage factory that is select
committee consideration—something that he  can proudly stand up and defend. The
communication principles will be one area that we will be looking at closely.
Then there will be the offences. Clause 18 of the bill sets out an offence provision.
The question will be asked, of course, of why we do not just resort to contempt of court
provisions. If it is an offence to breach an or der, why do we need to have this offence
provision that requires separate enforcement? If the court has made an order and it is
breached, then that is a contempt of court, so the existing contempt of court provisions,
I would have thought, would apply.
Let us examine that and look at it a little mo re closely. In clause 19 there is a very
interesting and, I would say, infelicitous use of the English language. One of the
14750 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14 Nov 2013
questions posed in clause 19( 1)(b) is whether a person comm its an offence if “posting
the communication would cause harm to an ordinary reasonable person …”. So we no
longer have just a reasonable person; it is an ordinary reasonable person. I do not know
what the difference is between an extraordinary reasonable person or a reasonable
person who is no longer ordina ry. I think we will need to tease out exactly what that
means. I would hate to be considered to be  just an ordinary reasonable person. I think I
am a reasonable person, but I do not think I am necessarily an ordinary reasonable
person, nor do I want to be considered an extraordinary reasonable person. So let us
understand exactly what that is, because we wa nt this legislation to  be meaningful and
to speak to the vast bulk of people who are goi ng to be looking to it for some sort of
protection.
We know what the ill is that this bill is trying to remedy. It is the nasty, ugly stuff
that goes up on Facebook, on other social media, on blog sites, and on other things.
People can be not just offende d but harmed, seriously harmed, by some of the things
that are put up. This is not a recipe for cal ling those in public office to account. I think
people in public office stand in a separa te category, but people who are going about
their daily lives—ordinary c itizens, who can make mistakes or who can attract
commentary and criticism—should not be beaten up in these fora, which are now so
public, so widespread, and so easily accessible. We understand all that.
I want to finally just refer to the safe ha rbour provisions that the Associate Minister
talked about. We think they are a sensible measure, a sensible protection for the internet
service providers. They should not be caught up, at least in the in itial complaint phase
that will take place under this legisla tion, but, of course, they do have some
responsibilities. We need to know that the internet service providers and the hosts, once
damaging and harmful material is drawn to their attention, understand that their duty, if
only a moral one, is to respond with alacrity to remove it or to at least suspend
broadcast of the posts and of the material until, if there is to be court action or some sort
of application under this bill, that at least is resolved. Those are sensible provisions, and
I can see that we would be quite happy to support those.
I think this will be a useful contribution. Th ere are some contentious issues here. Let
us see whether we can get around the ta ble and resolve them, and make this a
meaningful and workable set of provisions for the people who are looking to it for the
protection of their reputations and their dignity.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is always a pleasure to follow the
reasonably unordinary, reasonable Andrew Litt le, and it will be good to have him back
on the Justice and Electoral Committee to c onsider this very useful and good piece of
legislation, the Harmful Digital Communicati ons Bill, which has been introduced into
the House.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: Why, what’s wrong with me?

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I think the Hon Maryan Street needs to be there as well. But
what I am suggesting to the member is that  we are missing him from the committee. It
is often appropriate I think, usually, that the justice spokesperson for a serious party
should sit on the Justice and Electoral Committee. But, however, in this case usually we
do not see too much of him, but he will be welcomed back for this piece of legislation.
Bullying, sadly, has been around since time im memorial, really. The difficulty with
bullying in the past has been how to track it down, how to stop it, a nd how to control it.
But one of the challenges that those of us who were not born digital natives have is that
we were raised, through our adolescence a nd our teenage years, in an environment
where we were not subjected to harassment by digital technology.
Simon O’Connor: Some of us are younger.
14 Nov 2013 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14751

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Some of my colleagues are, of course, younger. But today we
find that for most people under the age of about 30, I guess, they are what we now know
as digital natives. They have grown up in an  environment where, sadly, it has been a lot
easier to partake in bullying and abuse, and far worse, by the use of cyberspace,
Facebook, the internet, texts, and all those modern communications. The purpose of this
bill, of course, is to mitigate the harm caused to people by digital communications and
to provide victims of that harm with a quick and efficient means of redress.
The trick, I guess, for this piece of legislation is, how do we manage that in an
environment that is, in many respects, a little bit like the wild west of technology? It is a
challenging conundrum for legislators, I su spect, all over the world. I am looking
forward, in the select committee, to seei ng what steps are being taken in other
jurisdictions, because I suspect  this piece of legislation ha s the potential to be quite
world leading. I suspect that there will be ot hers who will be watching closely what we
do.
The Law Commission has found that there could be as many as one in 10 New
Zealanders who has already experienced ha rmful communications on the internet, and
that for those aged between 19 and 29 the number could well be double that. There is
obviously a serious issue here. The La w Commission was doing work already on
harmful communications, as part of its repo rt on new media. The report was entitled
The News Media meets ‘New Media’: Righ ts, Responsibilities and Regulation in the
Digital Age . It was last year that the Minister of Justice, Judith Collins, asked the
commission to actually speed up their work and to fast track the work. In August of last
year she received the Law Commission’s recommendations Harmful Digital
Communications in the form of a briefing paper, and it was in this April that she
announced a suite of proposals to tackle cyber-bullying, which will be implemented
through this bill.
The main provisions of the bill are to crea te a set of 10 communi cation principles to
guide the approved agency that will be created under the bill , and that, I think, will be
something we will want to look at closel y in the select committee. But the bill will
create, essentially, a new civil enforcement regime that includes the setting up of this
new agency as a first port of call for compla ints. The agency will be able to investigate
and resolve complaints directly and very quickly, with the most serious complaints
being referred to the District Court, which can then issue what is known as a take-down
order, and of course they will also be able to put in place cease and desist notices. This
legislation provides a mechanism for people to quickly and easily request the removal
of harmful digital content from  websites, and blogs if necessa ry, and it also creates this
“safe harbour” provision.
I am very much looking forward to the se lect committee process. I am pleased that
the Labour Party is supporting this bill through  to the select committee, and I hope that
other parties across the House will do likewise. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: It gives me some pleasure to rise to speak to
the Harmful Digital Communications Bill.  Although it may have been a long time
coming, that does not alter the fact that it is here now, and I welcome that. We are
supporting it on this side of the House wi th some reservations. They are only
reservations that a nybody would have around this kind of issue, I think. I want to
outline three areas in particular that will need  careful scrutiny on the part of the Justice
and Electoral Committee, which the previous speaker, Scott Simpson, chairs so adeptly.
It is true, as Scott Simpson said, that th ere was a Law Commission  issues paper that
came out in 2011, but also last year the La w Commission’s minister ial briefing called

items.speaker: Harmful Digital Communications
items.text: The adequa cy of the current sanctions and remedies
came out. I think that that is a significant contribution to how we might get legislation to
14752 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14 Nov 2013
deal with issues that a decade ago people had not envisaged arising. Because of new
technologies, it is incumbent on this House to make sure that  we keep our laws up to
date. I think that my colleague Andrew Little put it well when he referred to the law
chasing, or having to keep up some pace with, some technological developments.
It puts me in mind of the time when I was serving on the Commerce Committee and
we dealt with copyright legislation. It was very difficult to get copyright legislation that
did not put people out of business and yet pr otected the rights of artists and creative
people, in particular, to their work. With  every exposure through digital media, the
copyright problem became more pronounced. It did not matter whether it was music or
writing; it became more and more difficult to get the law to fit.
This issue is not dissimilar. There is a se nse of the horse having bolted already, but it
is appropriate that this House turn its mind to it. We are all acutely sensitised to this
issue because of recent revelations about Facebook behaviour that has been nothing
short of despicable. Whether or not crimes  end up proven to have been committed, the
behaviour is despicable. I think that some  young people will find their reputations and
their career prospects destroyed because of  what they have indulged in by way of
Facebook revelations. That is a lesson to all young people, or will be in time, I think.
There are three things I want to cover. First of  all, I am particularly interested in Part
2 of the bill, which refers to the number of Acts that need to be amended by the passage
of this legislation. Fi rst of all, ther e is the Crimes Act, a nd that is almost self-
explanatory. There are three other pieces of legislation that will be amended simply by
the insertion of words that are to do with el ectronic communication or electronic media,
or words like “participation in fora for th e exchange of ideas a nd information.” These
pieces of legislation are the Harassment Act of 1997, the Human Rights Act of 1993,
and the Privacy Act of 1993. Each of these presents the select committee with a
different nuance, a different layer, of application of this bill.
The Harassment Act—fine, we are bringi ng that up to date by putting electronic
media and electronic communication into th e meaning of “harassment” as it is
expressed in that Act. That is a good thing because we are aw are of, and, as I say, at the
moment, acutely sensitised to, harassment,  bullying, and exposure of people in a way
that is despicable, as I have said. So the Harassment Act is going to be an important part
of the consideration.
The second important point, in my mind, is the amendments to the Human Rights
Act. Subpart 3 in Part 2 of the bill will amend the Human Rights Act. It will amend
section 61, which addresses racial disharmony; it will amend section 62, which refers to
sexual harassment; and it will amend section 63, which refers to racial harassment. That
is critically important because next come th e amendments to the Privacy Act. There are
provisions in the Human Rights Act that, w ith the addition of this bill and the
amendment by this bill, will really go to the heart of freedom of speech and the inability
of people to compromise other people’s right to exist peacefully. That is covered in the
Human Rights Act through a range of provi sions, and making electronic media or
electronic communications susceptible to th ose Acts is a good thing. We do not need
neo-Nazi, fascist websites to proliferate in this country. I am pleased if by this means
there will be some address of that. In other countries around the world we have certainly
seen such proliferation, and that is undesirable.
The third point is around privacy. This bill will amend the Privacy Act, but it is
going to be an area that requires consider able submission from interested parties and
real consideration of those submissions on th e part of the select committee. In addition
to that, we need to be caref ul around internet service prov iders, and we need to be
mindful of the impact of “notice and take down” measures on their services and their
ability to function as businesses. That is another area, and I hope that that business
14 Nov 2013 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14753
consideration will be represented by a subm ission from InternetNZ, because the bill
does impact on it.
I think that this bill is a worthwhile measur e. It has got some fish-hooks in it. It has
got very sensitive and far-reaching implications across other parts of our legislation. I
commend it to the House.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. I rise to take  a call in support of the Ha rmful Digital Communications
Bill. I think probably every member in this H ouse has been bullied at one point in their
life, just like every New Zealander. It is a tragic part of life, but what we are seeing with
online technologies is that it is a different kettle of fish from what it was even 10 years
ago, 20 years ago, or 1,000 years ago. We co mmend the Government for taking action
in this area. I think there is detail we will be looking through and engaging closely on
during the select committee process. But what we need to make sure is that our young
kids, particularly, are looking after themselves.
I note the clauses around—I have lost my wo rds for a minute; I think it is definitely
the end of the week, and I see the Serjeant- at-Arms standing there—inciting a person to
commit suicide. We have seen some absolute ly tragic accounts through the media. I am
sure many of us are familiar with cyber-bullying, which young Kiwis face. It is good
that the Government is adopting the Law Co mmission’s report after some tragic cyber-
bullying.
What we see is basically three parts in this legislation, three main provisions, the first
of which is the new civil enforcement regime to quickly and effectively deal with
harmful digital communications; secondly, a criminal offence being established, with
criminal penalties and new penalties there; and also some other subsidiary changes to
other Acts of Parliament.
What we also see from an informati on and communications technology perspective
is that—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the member, but the time
has come for the House to rise.
Debate interrupted.

14 Nov 2013 Business Statement 14701 
THURSDAY, 14 NOVEMBER 2013 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : When the House resumes on 
Tuesday, 19 November, the Government intends to move an urgency motion to progress 
a number of bills that are on the Order Pa per, including the Social Housing Reform 
(Housing Restructuring and Tenancy Matt ers Amendment) Bill and the Financial 
Reporting Bill. 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour—Rimutaka) : I wonder whether the Leader of the 
House could indicate whether the Government  expects there to be question time during 
urgency. 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : The Government has had 
question time through all of its bouts of urge ncy since coming to office. I imagine that 
discussions over the next couple of days with other parties in the Hous e will lead to a 
similar result. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Better Public Services Targets—Purpose and Impact 
1. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Finance: How is 
the Government’s Better P ublic Services programme contributing to a stronger 
economy? 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN (Asso ciate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of 
the Minister of Finance : Delivering Better Public Services has been a focus of the 
Government for the past 5 years. With th e Government representing around one-quarter 
of the real economy, it is important that Government agencies focus on achieving 
results for users of public services while at the same time delivering value for money for 
taxpayers. The Prime Minister last year identified 10 challenging Better Public Services 
results to address some of New Zealand’s mo st important issues over the next 4 to 5 
years, such as reducing crime, reducing long-term welfare depe ndency, and reducing 
educational underachievement. 
Simon O’Connor : Why has the Government made the Better Public Services 
programme one of its four priorities? 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN : The Government take s the view that New 
Zealanders are entitled to the most effective and efficient public services that can be 
delivered. The result areas are focused on improving Kiwis’ quality of life and getting 
better results for taxpayers. We have seen, for example, that the number of people 
continuously receiving a working-age benefit for over 12 months has fallen by almost 
3,500 since March last year to 74,600. The target is 55,000 by 2017.

MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT (REMUNERATION AND SERVICES) BILL 
Third Reading 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Attorney-General)  on behalf of the Prime 
Minister: I move, That the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Bill be 
now read a third time . The Members of Parliament (R emuneration and Services) Bill 
represents a significant improvement in m odernising the law relating to members’ 
remuneration and entitlement to services. The bill establishes a new framework for 
setting entitlements for members of Par liament and the executive. In doing so, it 
implements, subject to some modifications , many of the recommendations in the Law 
Commission’s report Review of the Civil List Act 1979: Members of Parliament and 
Ministers. The bill repeals the Civil List Act 1979—[Interruption]  
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (H V Ross Robertson) : Order! I am sorry to 
interrupt the member. It is a longstanding convention that members should not conduct 
conversations in the House unless it is nece ssary to do so and then only so as to not 
disturb the proceedings. Would members l eaving the Chamber please do so and show 
some courtesy to the member who is trying to address the House. It is good conduct and 
it is being considerate of others. 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON : Thank you. I will not name and shame Mr 
Twyford on this occasion. The bill modernises and modifi es the law relating to the 
salaries and allowances of MPs; support services provided  for MPs, Ministers, and 
certain electoral candidates; annuities and other benefits and privileges for former Prime 
Ministers; and benefits and privileges for former members of Parliament.  
As members know, the bill makes the Remuneration Authority rather than the 
Speaker responsible for determining accommod ation services for MPs and Ministers, 
and also travel services for family member s of MPs. It makes the Speaker responsible 
for setting directions on travel and communication serv ices for MPs and party and 
member support funding. Thirdly, it makes th e Minister responsib le for Ministerial 
Services responsible for determining any addi tional travel services  for Ministers over 
and above those set by the Speaker for MPs. This division of responsibility reflects what 
are intersecting interests here, one interest being that of having en titlements determined 
independently from those who receive them, an d the other being the democratic interest 
in the proper operation of the House and the ability of its members to carry out their 
functions. 
The bill also updates the legislative fram ework for the setting of salaries and 
allowances for MPs and Minister s. It addresses the current gap in the law relating to 
authorisation of the starting date for paymen t of salaries to MPs who enter Parliament 
mid-term, following the vacancy of a seat held by a list member of Parliament. The 
proposed amendment will allow these members to  be paid lawfully. The bill validates 
the commencement of salaries paid to mid-term list MPs since 1996, and it is a measure 
that will not incur further costs to the Crown. 
14718 Members of Parliament (Remunera tion and Services) Bill 14 Nov 2013 
The bill also substantially increases the financial penalty for MPs who are absent 
from the House without permission, with de ductions starting after 3 days’ absence and 
the amount deducted reflecting the member’s actu al salary rather than the salary of an 
ordinary MP. The financial penalty for absent  members used to be based on an ordinary 
MP’s salary. Now, in the bill, it is based on the actual salary of the member and, as I 
said, it commences after 3 days of absence, rather than 9 days’ absence in the original 
proposal.  
The bill introduces a financial penalty for members who are suspended from the 
House. The clauses covering financial penalties for members suspended from the House 
are new and reflect a recommendation made by the Standing Orders Committee.  
The bill also provides for entitlements to services to be determined in a way that 
takes into account the partic ular requirements of member s with physical or sensory 
impairments. As all MPs are aware, in recen t years there have been a number of moves 
to improve transparency around the costs of the House, and this bill codifies those 
moves. It imposes a statutory obligation on the general manager of Parliamentary 
Service and the Department of Internal Affairs to publish quarterly reports on travel and 
accommodation costs for both MPs and Ministers. It also imposes a statutory obligation 
on the Clerk of the House to publish quarterly  reports on MPs’ and parties’ use of the 
interparliamentary relations programme.  
The bill also addresses the operation of  the scheme providing certain former 
members with entitlements. As re commended by the Law Commission, the bill 
legislates for the former member travel en titlements of MPs elected before—take note, 
Mr Assistant Speaker—1999, thereby making those entitlements transparent and able to 
be changed only by legislative amendment. It introduces a statutory regime that sets out 
how these travel entitlements can be lost, including for various offences. It also imposes 
a statutory obligation on Parliamentary Serv ice to publish on an annual basis the travel 
expenses of former MPs. 
In conclusion, this bill makes a number of very sensible  changes, and these are done 
to ensure that the House and its members are properly supported in a way that maintains 
confidence in the integrity of Parliament. I commend the bill to the House.

removed from parliamentarians’ hands and given to the Remuneration Authority, which 
is independent, and I think that is the right thing to do.  
The issue of travel is very difficult because members of Parliament travel not just to 
and from Parliament but to and from their hom es to other parts of the country for work-

The purpose of this bill is to establish a new framework for setting entitlements for 
members of Parliament and the executive. It repeals the Civil List Act 1979 and changes 
the law regarding the salaries and allowanc es of members of Parliament, the support 
services provided for members of Parlia ment, Ministers, a nd certain electoral 
candidates, the annuities and other benefits an d privileges for form er Prime Ministers, 
and the benefits and privileges for former members of Parliament. Essentially, what that 
all means is that it modernises the regi me for giving members of Parliament and 
members of the executive the resources and to ols we require to carry out the tasks of 
being a member of Parliament and being a representative of the people of New Zealand.  
A number of members have said—those w ho have contributed to the debate today—
how these things have changed over time . One reason why the regime for pay and 
support services for MPs has changed is a de sire for greater transparency—a desire 
expressed both by the public and by members of Parliament. But another reason is 
simply the fact that the environment in wh ich members of Parliament operate now and 
the expectations of members of Parliament  have changed over the years. There was a 
time when members of Parliament did not re ceive resources to open an office in their 
electorate. They did not receive resources to  staff offices in their electorates and to 
provide services to their c onstituents, although most member s of Parliament did. They 
either funded it themselves or relied on vol unteers—often members of their family—to 
provide those services to their constituen ts. A decision was made, pleasingly, some 
decades ago that that was not adequate and our constituents deserved better service than 
that, so resources were provided to members of Parliament in order to provide those 
services.  
Likewise, with the advent of air travel and other forms of travel it was deemed 
appropriate that members of Parliament shoul d not only be able to travel to and from 
Wellington to carry out their functions here as  legislators but also be able to travel 
around the country to carry out their functions as representatives. This is because we do 
not just represent the people of our constituencies—although for those of us who are 
electorate members of Parliament it is our primary function, I believe, to represent those

interests of people across the country. Most of us hold portfolios of one type or another, 
and it is a requirement that we travel around and actually speak to the people working in 
those areas so that we actually have a grasp of what is happening at the front line, what 
is happening in reality, and we do not ge t stuck in the ivory tower that is the 
parliamentary complex.

recompensed for the work that they do. As Ch ris Hipkins rightly pointed out, I think, it

Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Minister of Labour) : I move, That the WorkSafe New 
Zealand Bill, the Health and Safety in Em ployment Amendment Bill, and the Mines 
Rescue Bill be now read a third time. It gives me great satisfaction to support these bills 
at the third readings. Following the releas e of the report of the Royal Commission on 
the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy in 2012 this Government committed to implementing 
the royal commission’s 16 r ecommendations by the end of  2013. By establishing 
WorkSafe New Zealand, strengthening worker participation arrangements in the mining 
industry, ensuring that the Mines Rescue service is adequately funded and supported by 
legislation, and paving the wa y for a new set of mining hea lth and safety regulations, 
these bills fulfil key elements of that commitment.  
Both the royal commission and the Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and 
Safety recommended that a new regulator be established in the form of a Crown agent. 
A stand-alone agency sufficiently resourced and with an executive board with a wide 
range of skills and experience will have the necessary focus to help reduce New 
Zealand’s high rate of fatalities and serious injuries in the workplace. But just creating a 
new agency is not enough on its own. The es tablishment of WorkSafe New Zealand is 
just one aspect of the most  significant reforms to the wo rkplace health and safety 
system in a generation.  
As I announced recently, this Government in tends to introduce a replacement for the 
Health and Safety in Employment Act,  which is now over 20 years old. The new 
legislation will be supported by a full spectrum of regulations, approved codes of 
practice, and other guidance material in support of the primary legislation. This was one 
of the areas that drew part icular criticism from the r oyal commission in relation to 
mining. The commission identified that ther e was a lack of supporting material sitting 
beneath the Health and Safety in Employment Act. So although duty holders knew what 
they had to comply with, they had no guidance as to how to comply. In the high-hazard 
industry of coalmining, this fact, among others, led to the tragedy at Pike River.  
The Health and Safety in Employment Am endment Bill will pave the way for a new 
set of mining health and safety regulati ons, as recommended by the royal commission. 
These regulations, among other things, will se t out the processes that  must be followed 
and the minimum standards that must be me t to safely manage the hazards that can 
cause catastrophic failure of the kind seen at Pike River. Mine operators will be required 
to develop detailed hazard management plan s to demonstrate how they will meet these 
requirements. These regulations will bring the regulation of mining health and safety in 
New Zealand into line with international be st practice. I would like to express my 
appreciation to both the expert reference gr oup that has been advising officials and the 
industry stakeholders who have engaged in a productive and ope n manner throughout 
the development of these regulations.  
The Health and Safety in Employment Am endment Bill also responds to another 
recommendation of the royal commission by significantly strengthening worker 
participation arrangements in the mining industry. The provisions of this bill will ensure 
14 Nov 2013 Mines Rescue Bill 14733 
that all mine workers at a mining operation, including contractors, subcontractors, and 
labour hire workers, will be covered by these arrangements.  
Health and safety representatives will be supported by a range of statutory functions 
and powers. Those who have undertaken prescr ibed training will be able to carry out 
inspections and suspend operations  if there is an imminent ri sk of serious harm. In the 
underground coalmining sector, which has seen the vast majority of  the fatalities in 
mining in the last 60 years, these strengthe ned provisions will be further supported by 
the appointment of industry h ealth and safety representati ves, who will provide, in the 
royal commission’s words, “an extra set of eyes and ears”.  
The Mines Rescue Bill responds to the recommendation of the royal commission 
concerning the mines rescue service. The bill clearly sets out the functions of the service 
and the legislation, and provides that the le vy to fund the service can be set through 
regulations. These changes will ensure that th is vital service is sufficiently resourced to 
assist mine operators with their emergency preparedness and to respond to emergencies 
and other incidents when required.  
This bill also provides statutory support for the role of the incident controller in a 
major underground mining emergency. This is a key role in the inter-agency protocol 
that has been developed in response to another of  the royal commission’s 
recommendations. The incident controller will lead the decision making at the mine site 
during an emergency. This legislation will ensure that he or she can effectively carry out 
this important task.  
It is our duty to the 29 workers who di ed, and their families, to oversee the 
implementation of the royal commission’s recommendations. It is also a duty we owe to 
all current and future workers in the mi ning industry in New Zealand. These bills 
implement several key recommendations of  the royal commission and I commend them 
to the House.

14 Nov 2013 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14747 
HARMFUL DIGITAL COMMUNICATIONS BILL 
First Reading 
Hon CHESTER BORROWS (Acting Minister of Justice) : I move, That the 
Harmful Digital Communications Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Justice 
and Electoral Committee to consider the bill. Rapid advances in technology over the last 
few decades have changed the way that pe ople communicate with each other. We now 
communicate with, form relationships with, and do business with people on the other 
side of the world. Our lives are increasingly entwined in the digital world. Smartphones, 
tablets, laptops, and desktop computers are everywhere. Smartwatches are also on the 
horizon. Modern technology has opened up a whole new world of opportunities.  
However, new technologies also present new challenges. It is now easier than ever to 
threaten others, spread destructive ru mours, publish invasive and distressing 
photographs, and harass people. People are bullied more easily, instantly, and 
anonymously. Bullying is no longer confined to  the classroom or the playground in the 
lives of young people. A digita l age has meant that tormentors can harass their target 
anywhere, at any time, and the trails of abus e remain in cyberspace for ever. Research 
suggests that as many as one in 10 New Z ealanders has personal experience of harmful 
communications on the internet. In 2007 it was estimated that one in five adolescents 
experienced some form of cyber-bullying or harassment that year.  
The Law Commission was asked in May 2012 to fast track its consideration of harm 
from digital communications. In August 2012 it made its recommendations on how to 
tackle the problem. I want to thank the Law Commission for its thorough work. The bill 
will give effect to the commission’s legi slative recommendations. I say “legislative” 
because there is already a lot of good wo rk going on to help combat the problems 
presented by harmful digital communications . For example, NetSafe is helping people 
to deal with these issues by providing users with the tools to protect themselves online. 
Schools are also moving to implement policies to deal with cyber-bullying. As the Law 
Commission notes, all of these are good m easures, but are simply not enough by 
themselves to tackle the problem.  
The Harmful Digital Communications Bill  provides for quick , effective, and 
proportionate responses to the harm caused by digital communications. The bill sets out 
10 communication principles to guide the work  of the approved agency for the courts. 
For example, “a digital communication shoul d not be threateni ng, intimidating, or 
menacing.” Let me be clear that this bill is not aimed at censoring debates and robust 
exchanges of ideas, or suppressing speech onlin e. Freedom of speech is something this 
Government and all New Zealanders value. Ho wever, free speech is not an absolute 
right. It must be balanced with other rights and freedoms. The bill strikes the 
appropriate balance between freedom of speech and protecting people from being 
bullied or victimised. It also requires the agen cy and the courts to act consistently with 
the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act to avoid any doubt about the importance of our 
fundamental rights.  
The first port of call for complaints about harmful digital communications will be the 
approved agency, which will he lp other people to  resolve disputes through negotiation, 
through mediation, and by providing advice. Th e majority of complaints should be 
resolved by the approved agency without any further need for action. This Government 
does not want people unnecessarily involved in the court system, especially our young 
people, who may be the victims or the perpetrators of harmful digital communications.  
However, for instances where the approved agency cannot resolve the complaint, a 
person can apply to the court fo r a number of civil orders. For example, the court could 
order a person to remove harmful content, i ssue cease and desist or ders, or reveal the 
14748 Harmful Digital Communications Bill 14 Nov 2013 
identity of an anonymous bul ly. The court will provide sp eedy, informal, and fair 
remedies, but will not be able to order fi nes or imprisonment. The most serious cases 
can be dealt with through the new criminal  offences of posting a digital communication 
with intent to cause harm, punishable by 3 months’ imprisonment; or inciting a person 
to commit suicide, punishable by 3 years’ imprisonment. To complement this new 
regime there are also amendments to existing law to ensure that they are fit for purpose 
and applicable online. For example, the Ha rassment Act is amended so that making 
contact online is explicitly included as an action that may constitute harassment.  
The final part of the bill that I would lik e to discuss is the safe harbour provision. 
This provision clarifies the law relating to websites and other content hosts, and 
provides people with an easy, acc essible, and direct way to remove harmful content. A 
content host could be any num ber of people—blog sites or organisations, including the 
likes of Facebook, Twitter, Vodafone, and TradeMe. Most of our legislation was written 
before the advent of the inte rnet and is not always clear about when a content host is 
liable for the contents posted by its users. Some recent court decisions suggested that 
the content host could be liab le for unlawful content that they do not even know about. 
Given the ease and speed of posting cont ent online and the volumes of information 
involved, the majority of conten t hosts cannot actually read and vet all content before it 
is published.  
The safe harbour operates via a notice a nd take-down regime. Broadly speaking, an 
online content host will not be liable for unlawful content that another person has posted 
on the website unless they are notified that the content is unlawful and fail to take 
reasonable steps to remove the content. The basic principles behind this safe harbour 
are, as with the rest of the bill, personal responsibility and fairness. The author of a 
harmful or illegal communication should be re sponsible for it. Content hosts should not 
be liable for things they have no knowledge of.  
This bill is not a silver bullet. It will  not stop overnight people bullying and posting 
harmful content online. It will, however, cr eate a First World regime to complement 
other efforts already taking place to effectively tackle harmful digital communications. I 
commend this bill to the House.

technologies, it is incumbent on this House to make sure that  we keep our laws up to 
date. I think that my colleague Andrew Little put it well when he referred to the law 
chasing, or having to keep up some pace with, some technological developments.  
It puts me in mind of the time when I was serving on the Commerce Committee and 
we dealt with copyright legislation. It was very difficult to get copyright legislation that 
did not put people out of business and yet pr otected the rights of artists and creative 
people, in particular, to their work. With  every exposure through digital media, the 
copyright problem became more pronounced. It did not matter whether it was music or 
writing; it became more and more difficult to get the law to fit. 
This issue is not dissimilar. There is a se nse of the horse having bolted already, but it 
is appropriate that this House turn its mind to it. We are all acutely sensitised to this 
issue because of recent revelations about Facebook behaviour that has been nothing 
short of despicable. Whether or not crimes  end up proven to have been committed, the 
behaviour is despicable. I think that some  young people will find their reputations and 
their career prospects destroyed because of  what they have indulged in by way of 
Facebook revelations. That is a lesson to all young people, or will be in time, I think.  
There are three things I want to cover. First of  all, I am particularly interested in Part 
2 of the bill, which refers to the number of Acts that need to be amended by the passage 
of this legislation. Fi rst of all, ther e is the Crimes Act, a nd that is almost self-
explanatory. There are three other pieces of legislation that will be amended simply by 
the insertion of words that are to do with el ectronic communication or electronic media, 
or words like “participation in fora for th e exchange of ideas a nd information.” These 
pieces of legislation are the Harassment Act of 1997, the Human Rights Act of 1993, 
and the Privacy Act of 1993. Each of these presents the select committee with a 
different nuance, a different layer, of application of this bill.  
The Harassment Act—fine, we are bringi ng that up to date by putting electronic 
media and electronic communication into th e meaning of “harassment” as it is 
expressed in that Act. That is a good thing because we are aw are of, and, as I say, at the 
moment, acutely sensitised to, harassment,  bullying, and exposure of people in a way 
that is despicable, as I have said. So the Harassment Act is going to be an important part 
of the consideration.  
The second important point, in my mind, is the amendments to the Human Rights 
Act. Subpart 3 in Part 2 of the bill will amend the Human Rights Act. It will amend 
section 61, which addresses racial disharmony; it will amend section 62, which refers to 
sexual harassment; and it will amend section 63, which refers to racial harassment. That 
is critically important because next come th e amendments to the Privacy Act. There are 
provisions in the Human Rights Act that, w ith the addition of this bill and the 
amendment by this bill, will really go to the heart of freedom of speech and the inability 
of people to compromise other people’s right to exist peacefully. That is covered in the 
Human Rights Act through a range of provi sions, and making electronic media or 
electronic communications susceptible to th ose Acts is a good thing. We do not need 
neo-Nazi, fascist websites to proliferate in this country. I am pleased if by this means 
there will be some address of that. In other countries around the world we have certainly 
seen such proliferation, and that is undesirable.  
The third point is around privacy. This bill will amend the Privacy Act, but it is 
going to be an area that requires consider able submission from interested parties and 
real consideration of those submissions on th e part of the select committee. In addition 
to that, we need to be caref ul around internet service prov iders, and we need to be 
mindful of the impact of “notice and take down” measures on their services and their 
ability to function as businesses. That is another area, and I hope that that business

commend it to the House.
